note:
The opening paragraph is written in Greek reminiscent of the classical style, the kind of opening expected in a literary book written for a wide circulation. Luke addresses Theophilus and explains his purpose for writing: to offer a well-researched and orderly presentation of the events that have launched the Christian movement, as a foundation for confident assurance in the truth of the gospel.

**1:1 many.** Mark’s gospel is no doubt included (and perhaps Matthew’s), but Luke is speaking of other sources for Jesus’ life composed in the first decades after Pentecost that have since been lost.

**accomplished.** The Gk. word includes the concept of fulfillment. The purpose of God for redemptive history reached its climax in the events of Jesus’ life and ministry.

There was reliable evidence for what was written, although Luke distinguishes himself from those who were eyewitnesses. The apostles’ pivotal role as witnesses of Jesus’ resurrection is stressed in Acts (1:21, 22; 2:32; 5:32; 13:30, 31). Jesus laid the foundation for their testimony by “many proofs” of His resurrection (Acts 1:3).

His research had gone back to the start of the Christian movement, the events surrounding the birth of Jesus Himself.

**most excellent.** An address for men of high social rank, probably belonging to Rome’s equestrian class, from which provincial governors were drawn (Acts 23:26; 24:2, 3).

The reliability of the eyewitnesses and Luke’s careful research and orderly presentation provide trustworthy grounds for assured conviction as to the truth of the Christian faith.

**taught.** The Gk. word is the source of the English word “catechism,” and it appears with a similar sense in Gal. 6:6. Theophilus had apparently received introductory instruction in the Christian gospel, which Luke intends his two volumes (gospel and Acts) to supplement and support.

Herod the Great, who reigned 37–4 B.C. Actually an Idumean, Herod had been appointed king of Judeaby Rome. His paranoia and ruthless violence in defense of his throne, even against his family members, are amply documented in ancient records.

**the division.** There was only one temple, and priests served in it on a rotating roster. The division of Abijah was the eighth of the twenty-four divisions (1 Chr. 24:10). Each ministered for a week twice a year.
The expression does not mean that they never sinned but that they were godly and upright people.

Like Abraham and Sarah (Gen. 17:17; 18:11, 12), Zechariah and Elizabeth are infertile because of age. To remain childless would be a serious disappointment to both and a source of shame to Elizabeth (1:25), for children are regarded as marks of God’s blessing (Ps. 127:3–5; cf. Gen. 16:4; 25:21; 30:1, 2; 1 Sam. 1:1–11).

The large number of priests serving the one temple meant that a priest’s opportunities for taking part in the ritual were few. He might not offer incense more than once in his life (some priests never had the privilege). This is the high point in Zechariah’s career. He would go into the Holy Place, after which the other priests would withdraw, leaving him alone to perform the offering on the altar of incense immediately before the veil leading to the Most Holy Place.
The incense symbolizes the prayers of God’s people (Ps. 141:1, 2; Rev. 5:8; 8:3, 4).
Probably the south side; the angel is between the incense altar and the golden lampstand.

This may be a prayer for a son, but more probably at such a moment, when Zechariah is ministering as priest on behalf of his people, he prays for the redemption of Israel. Either way, the answer to the prayer comes in the birth of Zechariah’s son, precursor to the Messiah.

**John.** The name means “the Lord is gracious.”

That he is not to drink alcohol has led many to think he was a Nazirite, but Luke does not say this, and there is no reference to John’s hair being left uncut (Num. 6:3; cf. Judg. 13:3–7). More probably, John had a unique position, neither priest nor Nazirite. He is the only person in the NT said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit from birth (vv. 41–44).

verse_quote: in the spirit and power of Elijah.
note:
See Mal. 3:1; 4:5, 6. Jesus identified John as the fulfillment of God’s promise in Malachi to send Elijah to make preparation before the great and awesome day of the Lord (Mark 9:11–13).

**turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.** See Mal. 4:6. John’s preaching will restore unity to broken families, undoing the effects of sin (Ex. 34:7).

**the disobedient to the wisdom of the just.** Going beyond the wording of Malachi, the angel predicts John’s mission will call Israel to repentance (3:2–18).

**make ready for the Lord.** The climax is that John will prepare the way for the Lord. By referring first to “the Lord their God” (v. 16) and then to “the Lord” for whom John will prepare a people, the angel identifies Jesus as the God of Israel (see 2:11). Elizabeth, on her son’s behalf, will acknowledge Jesus as “my Lord” before either boy is born (1:43).
Like Abraham and Sarah, Zechariah responds to God’s promise of a son with doubt (Gen. 17:17–19; 18:12–15). Mary’s question (Luke 1:34), on the other hand, expresses confusion but not unbelief.

Gabriel (Dan. 8:16; 9:21) and Michael (Dan. 10:13, 21; 12:1; Jude 9; Rev. 12:7) are the only two angels named in the Bible. That Gabriel (“God’s mighty warrior”) stands in God’s presence shows his greatness; such a one should be believed. The Gk. verb translated “bring you this good news” is the usual term for “preaching the gospel.”
Zechariah is granted the sign he seeks to confirm God’s promise but in the form of a mild judgment: he will be mute until his son is born.

The holy place. The people are outside in the temple court waiting for Zechariah to emerge and pronounce the blessing. Offering incense does not take long, so the delay is puzzling. When Zechariah does not speak but makes gestures (v. 22), the people conclude that he has seen a vision.
As the angel promised, Elizabeth becomes pregnant. Childlessness is considered a divine chastisement, but Elizabeth will bear this reproach no more (cf. Gen. 30:23).

More binding than a modern engagement, this is virtually a form of marriage. The couple do not live together or consummate their union, but a divorce is needed to break the relationship. See Matt. 1:18, 19 and theological note “The Virgin Birth of Jesus.”

Mary is humbled and puzzled that the angel should say she is “favored” (a correct translation of the word sometimes mistakenly rendered “full of grace”). The word indicates that Mary has received grace, not that she is the source of grace to others. Likewise, the “favor” that Mary has found with God (v. 30) is, again, grace—unmerited kindness., 29
The name means “Yahweh is salvation.”

There is a fuller meaning here than when the term was applied to John (v. 15). Jesus will be called “the Son of the Most High” by His Father (1:35; 3:22; 9:35) and even by demons, who know His true identity (8:28).

**the throne of his father.** Luke points to the Messiah as a descendant of David (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Ps. 89:29; see Acts 2:28–36).
The kingdom having no end is the kingdom of God over which the Messiah (Is. 9:6, 7), who is the Son of Man, reigns everlastingly (Dan. 7:14).

Mary understands the angel to mean something miraculous—birth without a human father. The virgin conception is a distinctively Christian idea. Greek myths relate stories of gods having sexual intercourse with women, but the biblical account of Jesus’ conception in the Virgin Mary’s womb is reserved in specifics and interprets this miracle in terms of creation and God’s presence in His sanctuary.

verse_quote: the power of the Most High will overshadow you.
note:
For the life-giving role of the Spirit at creation, see Gen. 1:2 (cf. Deut. 32:10–12). The cloud of glory (identified with the Spirit in Is. 63:8–10) “overshadowed” the tabernacle in the wilderness (Ex. 40:34, 35).

**holy—the Son of God.** The unique means of Christ’s incarnation is related to His exemption from the guilt and defilement brought by Adam upon all his descendants by his violation of the covenant of works in Eden. Jesus’ conception in a virgin’s womb also attests to His unique person as the eternal divine Son, who now takes to Himself a real and full human nature.

Elizabeth, and therefore Mary, was a descendant of Aaron (v. 5). The reference to “his father David” (v. 32) shows that Mary was also of Davidic descent. One of her parents was evidently descended from Aaron and the other from David.

verse_quote: nothing will be impossible with God.
note: A restatement of the Lord’s affirmation in response to Sarah’s doubting laughter at His promise (Gen. 18:14). See also Mark 9:23; 10:27; Eph. 3:20.
As the Lord’s slave (1:48 note) Mary expresses her faith in complete and ready submission to God’s will.
Mary must have left right away. Elizabeth was six months pregnant (v. 36); Mary stayed for three months and apparently went home just before John’s birth (vv. 56, 57).

verse_quote: the baby leaped in her womb.
note:
Filled with God’s Spirit from his mother’s womb, John begins his prophetic testimony to Christ even before his birth. His mother gives voice and words to the significance of his leap.

**filled with the Holy Spirit.** The Holy Spirit imparts prophetic inspiration to Elizabeth to declare God’s word concerning Mary and her son. See 1:67; Acts 2:4; 17, 18; 4:31.

Elizabeth articulates, in humble wonder, the true identity of Mary’s unborn son—“my Lord”—and pays tribute to Mary’s faith, which stands in stark contrast to the doubt of Elizabeth’s still-silent husband, Zechariah.

This song of praise, called the “Magnificat” (from the Latin word meaning “magnifies”), is revolutionary in its concern for the poor and despised of this world and its rejection of the rich and proud. Its focus is on the God who is about to intervene in power without regard for sinful humanity’s social order. Mary’s song echoes that of Hannah, whose son Samuel would anoint David as king (1 Sam. 2:3–8). It anticipates the preaching of her son Jesus later in this gospel (6:20–26; 16:19–31).
The word means “slave” and expresses humility (v. 38). Mary emphasizes God’s mercy to the poor and His holiness and power.

These acts of God are not necessarily or only in the past. The fact that God has chosen her, in insignificant Nazareth of Galilee (v. 26), to bear and raise His Son shows that the world system exemplified in Herod’s ruthless rule is giving way to God’s endless kingdom (vv. 32, 33). Mary rejects accepted ideas of privilege for the rich as she speaks of what God will do for the poor (Ps. 9:18 note).
By raising up the Messiah in keeping with His covenant promises.
God’s covenant with Abraham entailed both multiplying and blessing his offspring but also making him the avenue of blessing to all nations (Gen. 12:1–3; Acts 3:25, 26; Gal. 3:13–18, 24–29).
Jewish circumcision was on the eighth day (Gen. 17:12), but this is the earliest evidence for the custom of naming on that day.
A writing tablet was a board covered with wax. Writing was done with a pointed instrument.
Awe and reverence, appropriate to the presence of God, are evoked by the release of Zechariah’s tongue after months of divinely imposed silence. See 1:12; 2:9; 5:26; 7:16; 8:37.

verse_quote: laid them up in their hearts.
note: As Mary will do (2:19, 51), those acquainted with the circumstances of John’s birth recall and reflect on the extraordinary works of God.
As his wife spoke by prophetic inspiration (1:41 note), Zechariah begins to utter a poetic prophecy praising God and commissioning his newborn son for his work of prophetic preparation (v. 76).

A common way of beginning thanksgiving (Pss. 72:18; 124:6). The corresponding Latin term, _benedictus_, gives Zechariah’s song its traditional title.

**visited and redeemed.** As He did when Israel was enslaved in Egypt, God is about to visit (Ex. 4:31) and redeem (Ex. 6:6) His people. God’s people are not rescued without cost.

A symbol of strength (Pss. 18:2; 89:27; 92:10; 132:17).

**his servant David.** This phrase shows that Zechariah is talking about Jesus, not John, whose subordinate role is mentioned in vv. 76, 77.
There are several covenants in the OT, but the Abrahamic covenant was always seen as especially significant (Gen. 15).
As at the exodus, God’s people are liberated from their enemies so that they may be free to serve and worship Him in holiness and righteousness (Ex. 3:12; 4:23).
Zechariah turns his attention to John and says he will be the forerunner of the Lord.

verse_quote: salvation ... in the forgiveness of their sins.
note: Because Israel’s deepest plight is not about political oppression but about guilt before God, John’s mission and message will bring the knowledge of repentance that leads to forgiveness of sins (3:3).

This refers to the Messiah (Mal. 4:2). The Greek means simply “rising,” and some think of a shoot from Jesse (Is. 11:1). But the word is commonly used of the rising of the sun, so a reference to the dawn is more likely, particularly since John’s ministry fulfills the promise of Elijah’s coming to prepare people for the Lord’s arrival (Mal. 4:5, 6).

verse_quote: sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.
note: This imagery is drawn from OT descriptions of prisoners (Ps. 107:10, 14) and of those in Galilee to whom a great light would dawn with the gift of a son to rule forever on David’s throne (Is. 9:2, 6, 7).

verse_quote: grew and became strong in spirit.
note:
Possibly in the Spirit (of God), who has filled John from the womb. The description of John’s growth echoes that of Samuel (1 Sam. 2:21) and anticipates that of Jesus (Luke 2:40, 52).

**in the wilderness.** John grew up in the wilderness, also the location of his ministry of prophetic preaching and baptism expressing repentance and where God would now begin to form a new Israel (Is. 35:5–10; 40:3).

Luke dates the birth of Jesus by the then-common method of reference to political rulers (see 3:1, dating the start of John’s prophetic ministry). There is no other record of a worldwide census under Augustus, but he did reorganize the administration of the empire and conducted censuses for taxation purposes. Quirinius was governor of Syria when a census was carried out in A.D. 6 and may have been there earlier (10–7 B.C.). It seems to have been the custom to conduct a census at intervals of fourteen years. Luke may be referring to a census preceding the well-known and unpopular census taken by Quirinius in A.D. 6.
People went to their ancestral homes for registration, which made it easier to list families.
See note on 1:27.

The birth of the baby is described simply. “Swaddling cloths” were strips of cloth used to wrap a baby. That the child was put in a manger (a feeding trough for domestic animals) may mean that the birth was in a stable. There is a tradition that Jesus was born in a cave, which could have been used as a stable. Mangers were often outdoors, so it is possible that Jesus was born in the open air. Another possibility is that the place was the home of a poor family, where animals and humans often dwelt together.

**firstborn.** Jesus’ younger brothers and sisters, later born to Mary, are named in Mark 6:3; but this title also identifies Jesus as the preeminent heir in Jewish culture (Deut. 21:15–17; 1 Chr. 5:1, 2; Ps. 89:27).

**there was no place for them in the inn.** This may mean that the innkeeper did not want to have them there, or that lodging places were filled by others returning to Bethlehem for the census. Still, the detail foreshadows the rejection that Mary’s Son would endure (see 9:58; John 1:11).

Animals to be used for the temple sacrifices were kept in the open, even in winter. Despite the dignity bestowed on shepherds through God’s anointing of David (2 Sam. 7:8) and through His application of the title to Himself (Gen. 48:15; Pss. 23; 80:1), shepherds were a despised class by the time of Christ due to their transience and their work, which often rendered them ceremonially unclean. According to later sources, they were considered too unreliable to give testimony in the courts. Yet it was to shepherds that God first chose to announce the Christ’s birth.
In the NT, an “angel” is usually a supernatural messenger from God, as is this “angel of the Lord” who appears amid the Lord’s glory (see 1:11, 12, 19).
The Gk. phrase normally refers to the whole people of Israel (1:68, 77).

Astonishingly glorious titles are applied to this newborn baby. Jesus is called “Savior” only twice in the Gospels (also John 4:42; cf. Acts 5:31; 13:23). Roman emperors commonly ascribed the title “savior” to themselves, but Israel’s God insists that He alone is Savior (Is. 43:3, 11; 45:21; cf. Acts 4:12). “Christ” means “Messiah,” while “Lord” is regularly used in the Septuagint for God’s covenant name. “Lord” has already been applied implicitly to Jesus in Gabriel’s description of John’s preparatory ministry (Luke 1:16, 17).

The sign will enable them to find the baby, and it will prove to them the truth of what the angel said. The stark contrast between His humble crib and His exalted identity foreshadows the path of humiliation and suffering that awaits Him.
“Host” is a military term (1 Sam. 17:45; Is. 1:24), and it is remarkable that an army should announce peace (v. 14). The “peace” is peace with God, a peace that Christ will bring.

verse_quote: those with whom he is pleased.
note: Lit. “people of good pleasure,” referring to God’s good pleasure and merciful favor. As God receives glory in the highest heaven, where He resides, so the objects of His grace receive peace on earth. Compare the crowd’s praises at Jesus’ triumphal entry (19:38).
The shepherds immediately bear testimony, telling others the good news of the Christ’s birth and causing amazement in those who hear., 18

verse_quote: Mary treasured up all these things.
note: As did those who knew the circumstances of John’s birth (1:65, 66), and as she will when Jesus as a youth expresses awareness of His filial relationship with God (2:49–51).
Luke frequently recounts praise to God (5:25, 26; 7:16; 13:13).
Jesus is circumcised on the eighth day, as the law prescribed (Gen. 17:12; cf. Gal. 4:4, 5).

The need for purification arose from the mother’s being ceremonially unclean for seven days after the birth of a son. According to the Mosaic law, for another thirty-three days she was to keep away from holy things (Lev. 12:1–5). The mother was then to offer a lamb plus a dove or pigeon or, if she was poor, two doves or pigeons (Lev. 12:6–8). Mary gives the offering of the poor. The first male child of every mother is presented to the Lord, then redeemed through a substitute (Ex. 13:2).

Simeon was living by faith in God’s promise of a coming redeemer, as were John’s parents (1:6).

**the consolation of Israel.** This title for the Messiah refers to the comfort that He brings (Ps. 119:82; Is. 40:1; 57:14–19; 61:1, 2).

**the Holy Spirit was upon him.** As a prophet, Simeon received special revelation from God, first that the Christ would come in his lifetime, and then, when Jesus was brought to the temple, that the child was the promised Savior.
Simeon’s blessing is often called the “Nunc Dimittis” from the Latin, “now you dismiss” (ESV: “now you are letting ... depart”).
This phrase signifies the child who would bring God’s salvation to humanity. The abstract noun “salvation” is related to the personal “Savior” (2:11) in Greek as well as in English.

This phrase is plural and refers to the Gentiles as well as to Israel (v. 10 note; Is. 40:5). Both Israel and the nations will experience the Lord’s salvation not merely as observers but also as beneficiaries.

verse_quote: a light ... to the Gentiles ... glory to your people Israel.
note: God promised the servant of the Lord that he would not only restore Israel but also be “a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the ends of the earth” (Is. 49:6, cited in Acts 13:47). Jesus will be the one to fulfill this prophecy.

Mary also anticipated that her son would bring down the high and mighty and exalt the lowly (1:50–53).

**a sign that is opposed.** Simeon’s allusion to the servant songs in Isaiah brings into view the opposition and suffering that await Jesus in pursuit of His saving mission (Is. 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12) and that await the church in its obedient service to Jesus (Acts 28:22).
The sword imagery means that all this will not be without cost to Mary as she sees her son rejected and crucified (John 19:25).
Prophets were rare in Israel in those days, but the aged Anna was a prophetess.

verse_quote: fasting and prayer night and day.
note: Over her many decades of widowhood, Anna has relied utterly on God and served others through prayer on their behalf (see 1 Tim. 5:5).

Now an aged widow and prophetess, Anna, like the shepherds, bears witness to the Messiah’s arrival.

**waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.** This is another way of referring to “the consolation of Israel” (v. 25), since Jerusalem as Israel’s capital could stand for the whole nation (Pss. 122; 128; 137).
The Passover is one of three feasts that has to be observed in Jerusalem (Ex. 23:14–17; 34:23).

Jesus may have gone up with His parents every year, but Jewish custom specified that a boy should be taken to the feast a year or two before he was thirteen, when he would be made a “son of the commandment” (_bar mitsvah_) and become an adult member of the Jewish religious community.

Luke does not say why Jesus stayed behind or how Joseph and Mary came to leave Him behind, but travel in a large caravan would easily lead to the assumption that a boy was with his friends. If later custom was followed, the women and small children went ahead, and the men followed, so each parent might think a twelve-year-old boy was with the other.

The temple courts were commonly used for teaching. Jesus both listened and asked questions, showing a determination to learn. Jewish education emphasized the discussion of problems, which is perhaps behind the reference to “his understanding and his answers” (v. 47). But Joseph and Mary did not understand (v. 50); there is reproach in Mary’s words.

**your father.** Although Luke has shown that Joseph had no biological role in Jesus’ conception, legally and socially Joseph is the human paternal authority (vv. 33, 41) to whom Jesus willingly submits (v. 51 note) in obedience to the fifth commandment (Ex. 20:12).

Already at twelve years old, Jesus is conscious of a special relationship with His heavenly Father. The Jews do not customarily speak in this way. Jesus’ gentle reminder respectfully invites His mother to recognize that their parental claims are subordinate to those of God the Father (cf. John 2:3–5).

Notwithstanding His understanding of His relationship to the heavenly Father, Jesus is a dutiful son on earth and is obedient to Joseph and Mary as He grows. Mary does not understand fully, but she does not forget.

Luke notes Jesus’ well-rounded personal development as a real human being: intellectual, social, and spiritual. From the standpoint of His deity, He “knew everything” (John 1:48; 2:25; cf. Luke 5:20–22; 11:17), yet from the standpoint of His humanity, He increased in wisdom, as we do.

Luke’s lengthy chronological reference dates the beginning of John’s ministry, which was probably about A.D. 27–29.

**Pontius Pilate.** In his will, Herod the Great left Judea to his son Archelaus and other territories to his sons Philip and Antipas. But Archelaus ruled so badly that the Romans removed him in A.D. 6 and appointed their own governor. Pontius Pilate was the fifth governor of Judea, serving there from A.D. 26 to 36.

**tetrarch.** A tetrarch is a kind of petty prince. “Herod” here is Herod Antipas. Philip’s region is northeast of the Sea of Galilee. Nothing more is known of Lysanias, but Abilene is north of the other regions.

The Jews had only one high priest at a time. Annas had been deposed by the Romans, who appointed instead Caiaphas, his son-in-law. The Romans saw to it that Caiaphas exercised the official functions, but many Jews still considered Annas the true high priest.

**the word of God came.** John’s message is not his own but the dynamic word of God Himself.

The Jews baptized Gentiles who wanted to become part of the people of God. The sting in John’s practice was his call for Jews to undergo a rite they saw as fit only for Gentiles. John looked for a change of heart in Jews. See notes on Matt. 3:6; Mark 1:4.

All four Gospels apply Is. 40:3 to John and agree that John saw himself as only a herald. But only Luke adds Is. 40:4, 5, emphasizing God’s salvation to “all flesh,” that is, to Jew and Gentile alike.

A strong warning is directed at those who claim Abraham as father. Being able to trace one’s descent to the patriarch will not deliver from the coming wrath anyone who does not live in keeping with God’s law., 8

verse_quote: axe is laid to the root.
note:
This phrase points to certain, speedy, and imminent judgment.

**fire.** A symbol of judgment (vv. 16, 17; 12:49; Ps. 21:9).

The following verses (vv. 11–14) provide examples of what, for this crowd, were “fruits in keeping with repentance” (v. 8). The tunic was an undergarment; normally only one was worn. John suggests that the man who owns two should give the spare to someone without one, and so also with food (cf. James 2:15–17; Acts 4:34–37).

Roman taxes were collected by agents who bid for the rights to collect taxes in a city. They would pay the Romans what they bid and collect more for their own salaries. There was a strong temptation for them to enrich themselves by collecting much more than what was reasonable. Jewish tax collectors were despised as collaborators with the occupying Roman forces. They were excluded from the religious life of the synagogue and the temple. Yet Jesus enjoys table fellowship with them, and contact with Him transforms their grasping hearts (15:1, 2; 19:2–10).

Like tax collectors, soldiers were tempted to use their position to enrich themselves. John enjoins honesty and contentment on all. All four Gospels have an account of the ministry of John the Baptist as he called people to repent in preparation for the coming of Jesus. Luke alone tells us what John said to questioners who were uncertain about what it would mean for them.
Messianic speculations were in the air, but John says clearly he is no messiah. A greater one is coming.

In the rabbinic schools, a student did not pay his teacher. He was required to perform services but not the loosing of the sandal, which was considered too menial for a student and was reserved for the lowest of household servants. John recognizes his lowly place in contrast to the supremacy of the coming Christ (John 3:28–30).

**fire.** The baptism with fire points to judgment (v. 9 note). The winnowing fork (v. 17) is another symbol for judgment. Workers in Jesus’ day use the fork to throw harvested grain into the wind, letting the grains fall directly to the ground as the chaff blows away (Ps. 1:4). When the threshing floor is cleared, the chaff will be burned.

Although John’s warnings of impending and severe judgment are sobering, at the center of his message is good news, announcing the imminent arrival of the one who will bestow the Holy Spirit, the promised gift of the last days (Acts 1:4–8; 2:16–21, 33).

Herod Antipas divorced his wife and married his niece Herodias, who was married to his brother (Mark 6:17 note). John denounced this scandalous deed, so Herod imprisoned him in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea., 20

Jesus identifies Himself with sinners by undergoing their baptism.

**and was praying.** Jesus’ prayer during His baptism is mentioned only by Luke, who takes special note of Jesus’ prayer on other occasions as well (9:18, 28, 29; 10:21; 11:1; 22:31, 32, 40).

All four Gospels tell us that the Holy Spirit came upon Jesus at this time. Doves were important in the OT sacrificial system. Within that culture, they were regarded as affectionate and gentle. In Scripture, the dove is used often in imagery and comparisons, not always with the same meaning. See also Gen. 1:2; 8:8–12.

**my beloved Son.** In Ps. 2:7, the Messiah reports God’s address to Him: “You are my Son.” The Father now publicly declares the identity of Jesus, as Gabriel foretold it (Luke 1:35) and as the youthful Jesus implied it (2:49). The Father will repeat this declaration of Jesus’ divine and royal sonship on the Mount of Transfiguration (9:35). Satan will challenge Jesus’ sonship in the temptation that follows His baptism (4:3).

**I am well pleased.** To the royal connotations of “my Son,” God adds an allusion to the chosen servant of the Lord “in whom my soul delights” (Is. 42:1). This servant has received the Spirit to accomplish God’s purposes through His obedient suffering. Thus, Jesus fulfills both the prophecies about God’s Son who will rule over the earth and of the messianic servant of the Lord, who would suffer for His people (cf. Is. 53).

Luke’s genealogy differs from Matthew’s (Matt. 1:2–17) in going all the way back to Adam rather than just to Abraham. Some of the names differ, and the order is different. Some suggest that Matthew has Joseph’s line and Luke has Mary’s, but Luke specifically starts with “Joseph.” It may be that Matthew gives not direct ancestors but those legally in line for the throne of David, whereas Luke traces Joseph’s genetic descent back to David. Both emphasize that Jesus belongs to the house and lineage of David.

**3:23 about thirty years of age.** Joseph began serving Pharaoh at the age of thirty (Gen. 41:46), David ascended the throne at thirty (2 Sam. 5:4), and some Levites began their service in the sanctuary at that age (Num. 4:3).

**as was supposed.** As the account of Jesus’ conception in the Virgin’s womb has shown (1:27, 34, 35), the son-to-father relationship between Jesus and Joseph was not biological but rather legal and social or relational.

The term “son” is not in the Greek, but it is implied. Luke’s purposes in tracing Jesus’ genealogy back to the first man, Adam, are probably twofold: (1) to show Theophilus and other Gentiles that as the Messiah promised to Israel, Jesus brings salvation to all nationalities; and (2) to suggest a contrast between the temptation and failure of Adam the son of God in Eden and the temptation and obedience of Jesus the Son of God in the wilderness (4:1–13).

Jesus was “full of the Holy Spirit ... and was led by the Spirit,” showing that the temptation was in the plan of God. Right at the beginning, Jesus faces the question of what sort of Messiah He is to be.

The devil seeks to deflect Jesus from His divinely appointed mission. In His victory over Satan, Jesus binds the strong man and proceeds to plunder his possessions (11:21, 22). Luke’s account suggests parallels between Jesus’ temptation and the trials of Israel in the wilderness. Like Adam and Jesus, Israel was also called God’s son (Ex. 4:22, 23). Jesus is tempted for forty days in the wilderness, and Israel wandered for forty years in the wilderness (Num. 14:34). Whereas Israel failed the test of obedience in the Promised Land, Jesus, the true Israel, is fully obedient to the Father in His forty-day task in the wilderness of the land.

verse_quote: Man shall not live by bread alone.
note: In response to each temptation, Jesus cites Scripture, and all three passages are drawn from a section of Deuteronomy (6:13; 6:16; 8:3) in which Moses reminds the Israelites of lessons they should have learned in the wilderness. Jesus calls His followers to order their priorities correctly by focusing their hearts on the kingdom (vv. 31, 34).

verse_quote: a single hour to his span of life.
note: As the text note implies, this seems to be a mixed metaphor: a single cubit (a linear measure) to his lifespan (a temporal measure). Although the word rendered “span of life” can refer to physical height (as in 2:52), Jesus’ point, that anxiety cannot make even a negligible change, is better illustrated by the contrast of an hour to a lifespan of seven or eight decades than by the contrast between a cubit (18 inches [0.46 m]) to a man’s height (perhaps six feet [1.8 m]).
Solomon is known for his wealth and splendor (1 Kin. 3:13; 4:20–28).
The disciples are already in the kingdom. Therefore, they should concentrate their energies on the interests of that kingdom.

verse_quote: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy.
note: Central to this verse is the contrast between earthly goods, which are perishable and a source of anxiety, and the treasures of the kingdom of God, which are a lasting source of peace. Some of Jesus’ followers have at least moderate wealth (10:38; John 19:27; cf. 1 Tim. 6:17–19), and He is not demanding that all His disciples be poor. But they must be generous and not set their hearts on earthly possessions (v. 34), as is seen in the attitude and practice of the apostolic churches (Acts 2:45; 4:32–37; 2 Cor. 8:1–5).

That is, to be ready for service. Long robes hindered free movement and were kept above the knees with a belt when necessary. Israelites were to eat the first Passover meal with robes tucked into their belts and sandals on their feet, ready to leave Egypt the next morning (Ex. 12:11).

verse_quote: open the door to him at once.
note: The return of the Son of Man is certain, but its timing is unpredictable (v. 40), so His servants must be alert to welcome Him whenever He knocks. In His letter to the church at Laodicea, the risen Christ invokes this imagery: by His word the master of the house is knocking, and the servant who hears and responds readily will enjoy His table fellowship (Rev. 3:20).
This is a reversal of roles: the master takes the place of the servant (17:7–10; cf. 22:27), as Jesus will do by washing his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–15).
The Jews divided the night into three watches (Judg. 7:19) and the Romans into four. Jesus uses the Jewish division here. These servants watch for their master throughout the night.

In answer to Peter’s question, Jesus tells a further parable that shows that the principle of a servant’s readiness for his master’s return (vv. 35–40) applies especially to apostles and other church leaders, who have special authority and therefore heightened accountability to the church’s divine owner for their stewardship (vv. 47, 48; see Acts 20:28–31; 1 Cor. 4:1, 2).

The manager (or steward) was a slave put in charge of the whole estate by the owner (16:1; Gen. 39:4–6; 41:39–44). The owner was free from the burden of administration, and the manager had virtually universal authority over fellow servants and the owner’s property.
The reward of faithful service is the opportunity to perform higher service (19:11–18).
The punishment will be severe for those who treat the Son of Man’s apparent delay as pretext to abuse their authority or to become self-indulgent with God’s resources., 46

People are punished for failing to do right as well as for doing wrong. Ignorance can be blameworthy when there is opportunity to know what is required. God makes His people’s duty plain (Rom. 1:20; 2:14, 15).

**much will be required.** Just as towns that witnessed Jesus’ miracles were more culpable for their unbelief than notoriously wicked OT cities (10:13, 14), so those who have received more instruction (such as the apostles and the church’s teachers generally) deserve greater punishment should they fail to do the master’s will (v. 41 note)., 48
The fire of judgment.

Jesus’ death is also a baptism, another image that points to death (Mark 10:38, 39), as the floodwaters of Noah’s day destroyed the wicked and Egypt’s hosts perished in the waters of the Red Sea. Liturgically, Christian baptism symbolizes death to an old way of life and rising to a new way (Rom. 6:3–11; Col. 2:11, 12). Jesus accepts His death as the divine plan for bringing salvation to sinners.

**accomplished.** On the cross, Jesus speaks of the completion of His work (John 19:30).

As Simeon (2:34, 35) and John the Baptist (3:16, 17) anticipated, Jesus’ coming precipitates a winnowing of believers from unbelievers in Israel, and the division often cuts across family ties, as the gospel continues to do in each generation.
The people can discern that a west wind (from the Mediterranean) means rain and a south wind (from the desert) means heat. But they do not discern what God is doing in their midst.

In legal matters, anyone with a weak defense does well to secure an out-of-court settlement before the case comes to trial. Sinners should be reconciled to God now; they will perish if they wait until judgment day.

To kill people in the act of worship is a grave offense. This incident, not recorded elsewhere, and similar acts of violence recorded by other first-century historians contributed to Pilate’s reputation for cruelty.

Disaster is commonly held to be the result of extraordinary wickedness (John 9:1, 2; cf. Job 4:7–9; Ps. 73:2–14), but Jesus denies that one may deduce from this disastrous event that these Galileans were more sinful than others.

All are sinners, so Jesus calls on His hearers to repent—otherwise they will perish. The Galileans and those crushed by the Siloam tower had no time to repent at the time of their deaths, and Jesus’ unrepentant hearers might also face deaths that will give them no time to prepare. See theological note “Repentance” on p. 1964.
This incident is unknown to us apart from this passage. The tower was probably on Jerusalem’s southern wall, near the pool of Siloam (John 9:7).

verse_quote: a fig tree planted in his vineyard.
note: In the OT prophets, both the fig tree and the vineyard are symbols of Israel (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13; 24:1–10; Is. 5:1–7). A vineyard was fertile soil for a fig tree, and “three years” points to an established tree. It is unlikely that it would ever bear fruit, but its owner gives it one more chance. In His later parable of the wicked tenants, Jesus implies that He, the “beloved son,” has come as God’s final messenger to claim the fruit of the Lord’s vineyard from those who have mistreated servants (prophets) sent previously (Luke 20:9–18). That God does not punish sinners immediately does not mean that He approves of their sin. Rather, His patience shows that He is merciful, and that they should repent while there is time.
The right use of the Sabbath is a continuing dispute between Jesus and His enemies (6:1–11; 14:1–6).

The woman does not ask for healing. Jesus takes the initiative.

**13:11 a disabling spirit ... She was bent over.** Although the Gospels distinguish physical diseases from demon possession (Mark 1:32, 33), they also attribute a variety of physical symptoms to the dominating influence of evil spirits (Luke 8:29; 9:39–42; 11:14). As her contorted physical posture has visibly displayed her spiritual bondage for eighteen years, Jesus now releases her from “this bond” (v. 16).
The natural response from those who have experienced or witnessed Jesus’ miracles (5:26; 7:16; cf. 4:15). The people will join her joyful praise (v. 17).

See note on 8:41.

**Come on those days and be healed.** Since the woman’s condition has lasted eighteen years, it is clearly not life threatening, and her release could be postponed to an ordinary weekday on which work could be done. Jesus, however, contends that release from bondage is especially fitting on the Sabbath (vv. 15, 16).
The Jews released and watered their animals on the Sabbath as on other days, but this ruler of the synagogue objects to Jesus’ act of compassion for this woman.

This woman alone is identified by this title in the Bible (cf. 19:9). Jesus stresses her privilege as a member of God’s covenant community (Gal. 3:26–29), perhaps alluding to God’s promise to Abraham that his descendants would be freed after centuries of bondage (Gen. 15:12–14).

**loosed from this bond.** Jesus uses the same Gk. word to refer to the untying of an ox or a donkey to water it and the loosing of the woman from bondage to the evil spirit. Since the Sabbath commemorates not only God’s creation week (Ex. 20:11) but also Israel’s release from slavery (Deut. 5:15), the Sabbath is the perfect day to liberate Abraham’s daughters.

verse_quote: his adversaries were put to shame.
note: Jesus’ exposure of His critics’ double standard and His reasoning from the true significance of the Sabbath are unanswerable (14:6).

The brief parables of the mustard seed and the leaven, which illustrate the imperceptible but irrepressible growth of God’s kingdom, are gathered by Matthew (ch. 13) and Mark (ch. 4) with other parables. Their placement here in Luke’s gospel underscores the urgency of entering the kingdom immediately through the “narrow door” of repentant faith (vv. 22–30), though many (such as the synagogue ruler; v. 14) will not notice the signs that the kingdom has come.
A large amount; in Greek, three _sata_ (Hb. _seah_), equivalent to about three-fifths of a bushel (22 liters). Alsothe amount used by Sarah (Gen. 18:6).
See note on 9:51. Luke presents Jesus as making unhurried progress toward Jerusalem where the climax will be reached. On the way He continues to serve the people.

The Jews in Jesus’ day generally agree that all Israel (except for a few especially sinful people) would be in the number of the saved. This questioner senses that Jesus is drawing distinctions among the descendants of Abraham and Israel (2:34, 35; 3:17; 9:23–27) and that entrance into God’s kingdom will entail a personal commitment to Jesus that many will find too costly.

This does not mean that salvation is by works; it is a strong way of saying that people must be in earnest about salvation because the opportunity to receive it will not last indefinitely.

**narrow door.** Jesus does not say what the narrow door is, but clearly He is speaking of the way to salvation.

There is a time limit to the offer of salvation; it must be accepted while the offer is present.

**I do not know where you come from.** Cf. Matt. 7:23; 25:12.

To have social fellowship with Jesus and to hear His teaching are not enough. In fact, to witness His miracles and hear His words without responding in faith actually compounds people’s guilt (10:13–15)., 27

There will be weeping in grief and gnashing of teeth in anger as they see the patriarchs and prophets, with whom Israelites had always identified, blissfully enjoying God’s kingdom blessings while they themselves are thrown out.

As many who pride themselves on their covenant status as Abraham’s children will be excluded through unbelief, Gentiles from all nations will be included at God’s banqueting table through faith, fulfilling the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 12:1–3). Jesus will soon tell a parable in which guests invited to a banquet make excuses when the feast is ready, while outcasts from city streets and the countryside are welcomed to God’s table (Luke 14:15–24; cf. 16:19–31).

**recline.** This imagery of the messianic banquet describes the great joy there will be in the kingdom (14:15; Rev. 19:9). There will be a complete reversal of many ideas strongly held among humankind (v. 30).

Jesus may be in Perea where Herod is ruling. The Pharisees prefer to see Him in Judea where they have more influence, but Jesus will not succumb to fear or let threats from human rulers divert Him from the agenda assigned by the Father.

The Jews used the metaphor of a fox to mean worthless and sly. Jesus is unmoved by Herod’s threats and says He will continue with His ministry. There is a limit to the remaining time of His ministry on earth, as the reference to the third day shows.
There is a compelling divine necessity to what Jesus is doing (9:22; 24:26, 44–49). Notice also the further reference to the certainty that Jerusalem is the place where He will die (cf. 9:31).

This lament over the city is probably uttered as Jesus reaches the city (Matt. 23:37, 38) and is included here by Luke because of its relevance to what Jesus has just said.

**13:34 How often.** Jesus must have been in Jerusalem more often than the Synoptic Gospels explicitly report; the gospel of John records several visits.

**as a hen gathers her brood.** Although rejection and treachery await Him in Israel’s capital, in compassion Jesus stands ready to place Himself between an unwilling people and their coming destruction. The psalmists portray God’s providential care in the imagery of protective wings (Pss. 61:4; 91:4). See note on Matt. 23:37–39.

**13:35 your house.** This may mean the temple or the city as a whole. Both were destroyed by Roman forces in A.D. 70.

**until you say, “Blessed is he.”** Crowds would greet Jesus with this blessing from Ps. 118:26 at His triumphal entry (19:38), but here Jesus is looking beyond His death and resurrection. Some interpret this as a promise of an end-time conversion of the Jews (Rom. 11:25–32 and note), but the context may point more to the judgment of national Israel and the extension of the promises to spiritual Israel, made up of Gentiles as well as Jews (vv. 27–29). See Rom. 9–11 and notes.
Evidently to detect any violation of Sabbath observance.
A disease in which fluid collects in the cavities of the body (mentioned only here in the NT).

Although the lawyers and Pharisees (perhaps including His host) are watching and not speaking, Jesus reads their minds and hearts and again takes the initiative to challenge their restrictive view of the Sabbath (6:6–11; cf. 5:22).

**Is it lawful.** The law of Moses does not forbid healing on the Sabbath, but the “traditions of the elders” (Mark 2:16 note) prohibit medical treatment unless the condition was life threatening.

The Jews will pull a child or an animal out of a well on the Sabbath, though technically this is work. Their acts in an emergency show that deeds of mercy are lawful on the Sabbath and that Jesus has performed a deed of mercy.

Jesus is not offering a self-serving strategy for achieving recognition by feigning self-deprecation. He is advocating genuine humility that waits for eschatological vindication in dependence on God’s gracious gift, as v. 11 shows (cf. 18:14; Matt. 23:12).

verse_quote: invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind ... they cannot repay you.
note: As guests must renounce self-interest in selecting seating at the banquet table, so the host must renounce self-interest by welcoming outcasts whose presence will not bring him social or financial benefit. Ancient biblical wisdom assured those who loaned to the poor that God Himself would repay their investment (Prov. 19:17). In the banqueting parable that follows, Jesus portrays God Himself as welcoming “the poor and crippled and blind and lame” to dine at His kingdom banquet (Luke 14:21)., 14

This pious and conventional utterance, perhaps meant to change the subject, is evoked by Jesus’ mention of “the resurrection of the just” (v. 14) and expresses the sentiment that the kingdom of God belongs to a comfortably distant future. Jesus’ parable of the great banquet dramatizes the reality that God’s invitation into His kingdom celebration is going out in the present, and no pretext for declining His urgent summons is an acceptable excuse.

**everything is now ready.** Evidently those invited accepted the invitation; none is said to have declined. A second invitation on the banquet day itself, when the food is ready, is customary (cf. Esth. 5:8; 6:14)., 17

The excuses are transparently dishonest. No one buys a field or oxen without prior inspection, and if anyone did, there is no hurry—the field and the oxen will be there tomorrow. The man who had married might cite Deut. 24:5, but that freed a man from military service, not social contacts. Even within Israel, which received God’s first invitation through the OT Scriptures, those who value commerce or family more than Jesus’ call to commune with Him (vv. 25–33) will be displaced by those who know their need and heed His summons.

This parable is a prophecy of the extension of the gospel to those the Pharisees thought unworthy. The “poor and crippled and blind and lame” (v. 21; cf. v. 13) represent the despised Jews who are not able to observe the traditional laws of ritual purity (sometimes called “the people of the land”), while those outside the city along the “highways and hedges” (v. 23) represent the Gentiles. The parable concludes with a warning to the elite of Israel who reject the Messiah that they will not be given a second chance.

In contrast to rabbinic tradition, which permits hatred of one’s enemies (particularly Gentiles outside the covenant), Jesus calls His followers to love their enemies (Matt. 5:43–46). Clearly, then, He is not demanding that we hate our family members in the conventional sense of hatred. Rather, through this shocking hyperbole, He teaches that being His disciple means loving Him so unreservedly that all other loves seem to be hatred by comparison.
The implement of violent death, representing utter renunciation of one’s rights and life itself in the cause of God’s kingdom (v. 33). See note on 9:23–25.
Calculating the cost is important before undertaking any serious project. The “tower” could be a watchtower or a farm building. That one must “sit down” points to a careful and unhurried process.

A flavoring agent and a preservative. The salt in use at this time is far from pure, and it is possible for the sodium chloride to leach out of it, leaving a residue that is useless. Just as salt devoid of its distinctive taste is worthless, so a would-be disciple who evades Jesus’ demand of utter self-renunciation—the distinctive hallmark of allegiance to Him (v. 33)—is of no use in His kingdom.

See note on 3:12. Jesus regularly associates with tax collectors and other noteworthy violators of God’s law, seeing such outreach as intrinsic to His mission from the Father (5:27–32; 7:29, 34; 19:2–10) and offering them God’s forgiveness (18:9–14; cf. 7:28, 29).

**sinners.** The immoral or those who followed occupations that the scribes held to be incompatible with keeping God’s law. A rabbinic opinion stated that “one must not associate with an ungodly man,” and the rabbis would not even teach such a person. Notice that ch. 14 ends with “let him hear,” and ch. 15 begins with these “sinners” gathering around to hear Jesus.

Although Jesus tells three stories of lost things (sheep, coin, son/brother), Luke introduces them with the singular “parable.” It is implied that the first two establish a general principle (when the lost is found, joyful celebration ensues) as backdrop to the third, in which the older brother (like the Pharisees and scribes) refuses to enter into the joy befitting the recovery of what has been lost. The rabbis taught that God would welcome a penitent sinner, but the first two parables teach that through Jesus, God is seeking out sinners.

**15:3–7** Through Ezekiel, the Lord promised to come and fulfill the shepherding responsibilities that Israel’s shepherds (both the kings and priests in Ezekiel’s day and the scribes now criticizing Jesus) had neglected: “I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed” (Ezek. 34:16). In a different setting, Jesus uses the same parable to call leaders of His church to be proactive in protecting and retrieving members who go astray (Matt. 18:10–14).

The Gk. drachma (occurs only here in the NT) is equivalent to the Roman denarius, about a day’s wage for a laborer. The ten coins may have been the woman’s life savings, or they may have been strung together as a headdress.

**light a lamp.** Houses had no windows or perhaps small ones, so a lamp was needed even in the daytime.

The parable of the prodigal son could be called the “parable of the welcoming father.” While the repentance of the son is important to the parable, the father’s willingness to forgive, and his unexpected actions (v. 20 note, vv. 22, 23) are a striking illustration of the fatherly love of God for wayward human beings. Unlike His illustrations of the lost sheep and lost coin, Jesus extends this parable to include the older brother’s self-righteous refusal to celebrate the finding of the lost, just as the Pharisees and scribes resent Jesus’ mission from His Father to seek sinners and bring them into God’s family.

**15:11, 12** According to the Mosaic law, the firstborn son is entitled to two-thirds of his father’s property (Deut. 21:17). Sometimes the father gives the rights to the property (which means that he could not dispose of it himself, though the son can sell it) and retains the income (if the son were to sell the property, the buyer would be unable to take possession until the father’s death). But to give a portion of the property to one of the sons before the father’s death would be unusual, and for a son to request it would be highly insulting to the father., 12

Swine are unclean (Lev. 11:7). Since no conscientious Jew would take this job willingly, the son’s willingness to do such work represents his indifference to God’s holiness, his utter desperation, or both.
The father is apparently watching intently for his son’s return. It is undignified for an older man to lift up his robes and run.

The father’s actions indicate complete forgiveness and restoration of relationship. In his joy, he apparently interrupts the son’s rehearsed apology (vv. 18, 19, 21). The “best robe” is a mark of distinction, and the ring signifies authority (Gen. 41:42; Esth. 3:10; 8:2). Because slaves do not wear shoes, the shoes point to the status of a free man. The fattened calf is reserved for special occasions., 23
The older son’s attitude illustrates the judgmental spirit of the Pharisees who are offended at Jesus’ welcome of “sinners” (vv. 1–3).

The older brother’s refusal to participate in the father’s joyful feast, no less than the younger brother’s demand for his inheritance and departure to a distant country and dissolute life, insults the father’s honor and reputation. As with the younger son (v. 20), the father again takes the initiative in restoring the relationship, leaving his house a second time to heal the alienation that had distanced the older, obedient (as he saw himself) son from the father’s celebration. The parable as a whole points to the sovereign love of God, who actively seeks out unworthy sinners who do not seek Him (19:10).

The older brother views his relationship with the father as that of a slave who deserves reward for meritorious behavior. As the father’s loving response to the undeserving younger son shows, salvation is not a reward for good works but entirely the gracious gift of God (Eph. 2:8, 9).

verse_quote: all that is mine is yours.
note: Within the framework of the parable, the property settlement remains unchanged. The attitude of the older son (v. 29 note) has caused him to lose sight of the relationship he does have with his father. Jesus is not implying, however, that those who share the older brother’s resentment over divine grace to the unworthy can nonetheless be reassured that they are God’s heirs. Such resentment puts one in danger of becoming like those in Jesus’ day who cannot recognize the grace of the Lord.

verse_quote: was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.
note: The motif of fitting celebration when the lost is found ties the three stories together (vv. 6, 7, 9, 10, 23, 24). Jesus ends the parable without revealing the old brother’s response to his father’s appeal, confronting his critics with how they will respond to God’s lavish grace toward the undeserving.
The man who runs the estate, freeing the owner from being involved in every detail (cf. Gen. 39:5, 6). Because he is not closely supervised, he can easily be careless, lazy, or dishonest.

The manager may have shrewdly deprived his master of funds legally owed him by debtors as he prepared the financial records for a final audit. But Jews are forbidden to take usury, and one way around the regulation is to overcharge. The first debtor might have borrowed four hundred gallons of oil and had the bill made out for eight hundred, the extra being the equivalent of a high rate of interest. By reducing the amount of interest the debtor owed, the manager would have obliged the debtor to assist him personally (v. 4) without diminishing the principal owed to his own master.

With the original bills destroyed, the owner is in an awkward position. He cannot establish his claim to the full amount, which includes the interest. He praises the shrewdness of his manager, acknowledging that he has been outwitted. Jesus uses the parable to illustrate that worldly people often use what they have to further worldly ends more strategically than people of the light do to further the quite different aims of God’s kingdom.

Jesus’ disciples are to use what wealth they have not for selfish purposes but to “make friends.” Generosity to the poor is probably in view here, since God Himself will repay those who relieve the needy (14:13, 14; Prov. 19:17).

**receive you.** The text does not explicitly specify who is doing the receiving. Possibilities include the poor who have been helped in this life, or, more likely, God Himself. In either case, salvation by works is not being taught (15:29 note). The loving help given to others in this life is a fruit of faith and a sign of genuine discipleship and salvation already enjoyed rather than a meritorious ground of salvation.

Financial resources exchanged in the commerce of this age are not intrinsically “unrighteous” (v. 9) or “dishonest” (reflecting the same Gk. word in vv. 8, 10). But “wealth” or “money” (_mammon_ in vv. 11, 13) may compete with God for our trust and allegiance. Even when it does not, its value is “little” (v. 10) and short-lived when contrasted to eternal, true riches.

**true riches.** Heavenly treasures, also described as “eternal dwellings” (v. 9).

If “that which is your own” refers to the “true riches” mentioned in v. 11, then Jesus is saying that faithfulness as a manager in this life determines one’s reward in the heavenly kingdom (Matt. 25:34).
A slave is bound both to obey his master and to depend on the master’s protection and provision. Either the living God or money may claim one’s mastery, but not both (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

A reference to the entire OT.

**were until John.** Luke here indicates that the ministry of John the Baptist signaled the great turning point of redemptive history (Matt. 11:11 note).

**everyone forces his way into it.** A difficult statement to translate and interpret. Some suggest that Jesus is exhorting His followers by describing the zeal necessary for entering the kingdom (13:24). Others suggest that the verb rendered “forces his way” is meant in a negative sense, depicting hostile powers fighting against the kingdom (Matt. 11:12 note).
A tiny projection on some Hb. letters; it is the smallest part of a letter. The entire law comes from God, and it is as sure as its author (Matt. 5:17, 18 notes).

Jewish men at this time can divorce their wives easily and for slight cause. Jesus has a higher view of marriage; the law’s provision for divorce (Deut. 24:1–4) is due to hardness of heart (Mark 10:5). He sees casual divorce as causing adultery (Matt. 5:31, 32; 19:9). See theological note “Divorce” on p. 1755.
The expensive clothing of the rich. Purple is used for the outer garment and linen for the undergarment.
The only character given a name in Jesus’ parables.

Jesus says nothing overtly about the religious condition of either, but the fact that Lazarus is conducted by angels to feast with Abraham implies that he is right with God, whereas the rich man’s torment shows that he is not.

**Abraham’s side.** The image of “side” relates to being the guest of honor at a banquet (cf. John 13:23).
The usual Gk. name for the place of the dead. In the NT, it is not used with reference to the righteous. Here it is clearly a place of torment. See theological note “Hell” on p. 1753.
Even in Hades, the rich man is arrogant, thinking that he can have Lazarus sent to do his bidding.

The address “child” is tender, but it cannot alter the facts. A great chasm separates them, and there is a whole new order with a complete reversal of earthly values.

**your good things.** The rich man once had what he saw as good things. He could have chosen the things of God, but he preferred temporary material pleasures.
For the first time, the rich man thinks of others, though these others are part of his own family. And he still assumes that Lazarus may be sent to do his bidding., 28

A reference to the OT. The rich man assumes that the resurrection of a man from the dead (or visitation by a departed spirit) will turn his brothers from their self-indulgent lives. Jesus says they have the witness of the Word of God, as the rich man did while he was still alive. Having rejected the revelation already given to them, they will not be persuaded by a miraculous resurrection of someone from the dead. It is noteworthy that when Jesus actually raises a man named Lazarus, it does not bring His opponents to repentance (John 11:46–53; 12:9–11).
The Gk. word originally designated the bait stick of a trap; it came to mean anything that trips or traps people (text note).
Children or humble believers (cf. 10:21), who are helpless apart from God’s aid.
The obligation to forgive even when a brother sins repeatedly is based in the reality that God has forgiven us a massive debt that we could never repay (Matt. 18:21–35).

Apparently, the apostles think great faith is needed to be so forgiving. Jesus points to what even small faith can bring about. More important than the quantity of faith is the object of faith—a great and powerful God., 6

In ordinary life, masters do not, and are not obligated to, relieve slaves of household duties merely because they have put in a hard day of outdoor labor. Yet Jesus has predicted such a reversal of roles in His kingdom (12:37, 38) and will enact it at the Last Supper (John 13:3–17; cf. Luke 22:24–27).

verse_quote: we have only done what was our duty.
note: As God’s servants we can never exceed, or even meet, our obligation to Him. This general principle is applicable here to the duty of forgiving a brother repeatedly (vv. 3, 4) which, in view of the grace we have received, neither demands extraordinary faith (vv. 5, 6) nor deserves extraordinary recognition.

People with leprosy (a term applied to various rashes and skin diseases) are ceremonially defiled with respect to Israel’s worship in God’s sanctuary and are therefore required by the law to keep away from people who are ritually clean (Lev. 13:46). These lepers come as close as they dare and call out loudly to Jesus.

Lev. 14:1–32 authorizes the Levitical priests to certify that a person formerly excluded from the community has been cleansed from his pollution. See note on 5:14.

**as they went.** Jesus’ command, when nothing has yet happened to the men, is a test of faith. They are healed as they go forth in obedience to Jesus’ word.

Gratitude brings back one man, who praises God for what had happened. That he is a Samaritan makes this all the more surprising, for he is not expected to show much gratitude to a Jewish healer. The antipathy between Samaritans and Jews is seen in a Samaritan village’s refusal of hospitality to Jesus’ entourage and in the readiness of Zebedee’s sons to retaliate (9:52–55; cf. John 4:9; 8:48). But in a parable, Jesus makes a Samaritan the sole individual who loved his neighbor as himself (Luke 10:30–37; cf. Acts 8:4–25)., 16

Jesus’ answer to questions regarding the coming of the kingdom of God points to the mysterious and dynamic character of that kingdom. In this passage, Jesus presents the kingdom both as a reality that is present (v. 21) and as a reality that has yet to be fully revealed (vv. 22–37). Jesus often presents the kingdom as a hidden and growing reality (Matt. 13:31–33), which is both present and future. In the earthly ministry of Jesus, the kingdom is already present (11:20), but the full reality of the kingdom is yet to be manifested (cf. 19:11). Christians are to pray for the full realization of God’s kingdom (11:2). See note on Matt. 13:11, 12 and the theological note “The Kingdom of God.”

verse_quote: the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.
note: Cf. text note. The translation “in the midst of you” accurately points to the presence of the kingdom in the person of Jesus. Jesus’ point is not that the kingdom indwells each of the Pharisees who have asked the question but that it is among them because He, the king, is present.

verse_quote: one of the days of the Son of Man.
note: A probable reference to the full manifestation of the kingdom at the second coming of Christ (vv. 26, 30). Christians long for the coming of Christ and for the peace and justice that the second coming will bring.

Though some will seek after false messiahs (21:8, 9), and reports may circulate that “the day of the Lord has come” (2 Thess. 2:1–8), the final coming of Christ will be so public that everyone will know.
The word “must” indicates that Christ’s suffering is mandated by the sovereign purpose of God (24:25–27, 44–49; Acts 4:27, 28).

People in the times of Noah and Lot carried on with the normal life of this world (Jesus does not speak of their sins) and neglected their opportunity to turn to God in repentance. Noah and Lot were sinners, but they heeded God’s warnings and were saved.

verse_quote: when the Son of Man is revealed.
note: His return will be not only unmistakably visible to all (v. 24) but also sudden and unexpected to many, offering no window of time for last-minute repentance.
Lot’s wife came close to deliverance, but her backward look in disobedience to God’s command doomed her (Gen. 19:26).
Jesus repeats the teaching of 9:24 that the selfish, self-affirming life means spiritual death.
Close proximity to some saved person will not help in the day of Christ’s coming., 35
Jesus apparently uses a popular proverb to teach that just as dead bodies attract vultures, so the spiritually dead invite judgment.

The preceding verses (17:22–37) and the reference to the second coming in v. 8 indicate that persistence in prayer for the coming of Christ and His final triumph over evil, even when that coming is seemingly delayed, is particularly in view (vv. 7, 8; 1 Cor. 16:22; Rev. 22:20). On the general principle that continued prayer is important in all matters, see 11:5–8 and notes.

verse_quote: neither feared God nor respected man.
note: Neither a sense of accountability to God, the supreme judge, nor concern for others’ opinions will move this unrighteous judge (v. 6) to render a particular verdict. Only bribery or another appeal to his self-interest can sway the judge’s decisions, and the widow has no resources to win his support.

As a woman without a husband or other male relative to press her case, the widow has no legal leverage and has nothing but right on her side. She seeks justice, not revenge, against a legal adversary who is exploiting her social vulnerability (Is. 1:17, 23).

Although the judge may mean that the woman will ruin his reputation, his indifference to public opinion (v. 2) makes this unlikely. Rather, he is graphically portraying the annoying discomfort caused by her stubborn persistence.

If even an “unrighteous” and reluctant judge (v. 6) will do what is right, how much more will God, who is eager to vindicate those whom He has chosen in His love?

**delay long.** God will not keep putting them off like the judge in this parable; any delay will have a good reason in His infinite wisdom. In general, what seems like delay to us is the outworking of God’s patience to gather all His elect through the preaching of the gospel (2 Pet. 3:9). We can be confident that He is working all things together for our good in every circumstance (Rom. 8:28).

This is in God’s time (2 Pet. 3:8), not ours.

**will he find faith.** This does not mean that there will be no believers but that unbelief and rebellion will be predominant in the “little while” that Satan is released after ages of gospel advance among the nations (Rev. 20:1–10; 2 Thess. 2:3–12).

If the preceding parable taught the necessity of persistence in prayer, this parable teaches that prayer is not automatically acceptable to God.

The shocking outcome of this parable—a tax collector justified and a law-observant Pharisee left unforgiven—is Jesus’ sharp corrective to those whose confidence in their own righteousness leads them to despise others whose keeping of the law falls short.
Personal prayers can be offered in the temple at any time of day, not only in formal services (2:37).
A common posture for prayer.

The only fast prescribed in the law of Moses is on the Day of Atonement (Lev. 16:29–31; 23:27), though voluntary fasting can accompany prayer (Ps. 35:13), penitence (1 Kin. 21:27), and mourning (2 Sam. 1:12). By the time of Christ, Jewish oral tradition has increased the number of fasts expected of the pious. Fasting can be a useful religious exercise (5:33–35; Acts 13:2, 3), but Jesus roundly condemns the practice when it is seen as a way of meriting God’s favor or when it is publicized through ostentatious display (Matt. 6:16–18; cf. Is. 58:1–6).

**tithes of all that I get.** The law required that crops be tithed by farmers (Lev. 27:30–33; Deut. 14:22–29), not the consumers who purchased those crops for food. This Pharisee boasts again of exceeding the demands of God’s law.

verse_quote: lift up his eyes to heaven.
note:
Looking upward is typical while praying, but this man is too conscious of unworthiness to do this. He simply asks for mercy as he acknowledges his sin.

**be merciful to me.** Not the customary term for showing mercy, but one descriptive of God’s turning away His wrath through atoning sacrifice. A related noun is rendered “propitiation” in 1 John 2:2.

The Pharisee relies on his own merits, not having discovered that no human righteousness is sufficient before a God who demands perfection (Matt. 5:48; Ps. 143:2; Rom. 3:20). The tax collector relies on God’s mercy and finds it.

As the Pharisee in the parable despises the guilty tax collector, so Jesus’ disciples devalue infants and seek to keep them from interrupting Jesus’ ministry to important, useful people (see 9:46–48). To receive the kingdom as a child is not to be innocent but to be utterly dependent on God, who shows mercy.

A general term meaning someone from the upper classes.

**Good Teacher.** This is not a usual form of address in Judaism; it is mere flattery. The man assumes that his deeds will bring him to eternal life. He exemplifies “some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous” (v. 9).

verse_quote: Why do you call me good.
note: Jesus is not denying His goodness but is challenging the ruler’s flattery by reminding him that true goodness is an attribute of God alone. The ruler’s estimation of goodness is too shallow, and his perception of Jesus is much too low. The insincerity of his flattery is shown by his failure to do what the “Good Teacher” teaches him (v. 23).

Instead of quibbling over the ruler’s claim to have kept God’s commands from youth, Jesus puts His finger on the idolatry at the core of the man’s being. This challenge reveals that the young man has not really understood any of the commandments. When he faces the choice, it becomes clear that his possessions come before God, a direct violation of the first and tenth commandments (which, strategically, Jesus did not cite).

See note on Mark 10:25. The wealthy are tempted to rely on earthly things, together with those whose wealth is achievement in intellectual, artistic, or other fields. Great achievers often find it difficult to rely wholly and humbly on the mercy of God.

verse_quote: a camel to go through the eye of a needle.
note: Jesus dramatizes with deliberate hyperbole how impossible it is for a rich man to enter God’s kingdom, presenting an absurd image to the mind’s eye. See note on Mark 10:25.

The hearers make the common mistake of assuming that wealth is a sign of God’s favor (Job 1:1–5; 42:10–17). Thus, what they are essentially asking is this: “If the rich with all their advantages cannot easily be saved, who can be?” Salvation, for rich or poor, is always impossible for humans to attain on their own, so it will always be the gift of God (1:37)., 27
Jesus’ answer to Peter means that God’s gifts surpass anything we can give up for Him. It does not mean that we should make sacrifices merely as a means of getting a better reward.
In His predictions of the Passion (cf. 5:35; 9:22, 43–45; 12:50; 13:32, 33; 17:25), this is the first time Jesus speaks of being handed over to the Gentiles.

Luke implies that Jesus is entering Jericho, whereas Matthew and Mark say the incident occurred as they “went out” of Jericho (Matt. 20:30; Mark 10:46). There seem to have been two “Jerichos” about a mile (1.6 km) apart in the first century: the ruins of the OT city conquered by Joshua (Josh. 6), and a city built by Herod the Great. The encounter may occur as Jesus is leaving the old city and entering the new.

**a blind man.** Matthew mentions two blind men (cf. Matt. 9:27 and note). Luke and Mark mention only one; he may have been the spokesman for the two.

A messianic title, implied in Gabriel’s promise to Mary (1:32) and grounded in God’s promise to David (2 Sam. 7:12–16; see Ps. 89:19–37). David himself is not associated with miraculous healing, but this blind man expects the Messiah to exceed his ancestor (Is. 42:6, 7).

Faith is the means by which the gift is received.

**has made you well.** This might be translated “has saved you,” which would fit in with his following Jesus and glorifying God—a typical and appropriate response to Jesus’ miracles (5:25, 26; 7:16, 13:13; 17:15).
The term is found nowhere else, but clearly it means the head of the local taxing agents. Jericho is near a major trade route. There is much to tax, and Zacchaeus is accordingly quite rich.
A tree frequently planted by the roadside; it is easy to climb.

verse_quote: I must stay at your house.
note: Jesus takes the initiative, since His mission is to seek and save the lost (v. 10).
Jesus is again criticized for associating and eating with sinners (7:34; 15:1, 2; cf. Acts 11:2, 3).

The verb is in the present tense for vividness and emphasis.

**fourfold.** The law requires restoration of the amount wrongfully taken, plus a fifth as a penalty (Lev. 6:5; Num. 5:7). In his joy over Jesus’ gracious initiative (v. 6), Zacchaeus goes far beyond what the law demands.

Jesus has said it is hard for a rich person to be saved (18:24, 25), but the salvation of Zacchaeus shows it is not impossible for God to rescue even the affluent from enslavement to their wealth (18:27).

**a son of Abraham.** Zacchaeus is one of the lost sheep of Israel, to whom Jesus’ mission is specifically directed during His earthly ministry (cf. 13:16; Matt. 10:6; 15:24).

verse_quote: to seek and to save the lost.
note: The recurring theme of the parables of the lost (15:3–7, 8–10, 24, 32).

Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem is nearing its end, and some believe He will soon expel Rome’s occupation forces and restore Israel’s political independence and military dominance (cf. Acts 1:6, 7). They misunderstand both the timing of God’s plan and the character of Christ’s kingdom (John 18:33–37).

The parable of the talents (Matt. 25:14–29) resembles this one, but there the amounts are larger (one talent = 60 minas) and vary in quantity (five, two, one), testing the servants for their fitness for larger tasks. Here the amounts are small and the same for all (v. 13). The parable teaches that everyone has one basic task—to serve God faithfully.

**a far country.** After the death of Herod the Great, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome hoping to be appointed king by Caesar Augustus. See note on v. 14.
Each servant receives one mina, the equivalent of one hundred drachmas (15:8 note), or one-sixtieth of a Gk. talent, representing several months’ wages.

A delegation of Jewish leaders protested Archelaus’s appointment as king to succeed his father, Herod, so Augustus gave him only the title “ethnarch.” Jesus may be weaving that incident into this parable as a subplot, with the twist that His own departure (to His Father’s right hand in heaven) opens an era in which His servants must invest His gifts, and His enemies may still, for a time, resist His rule.

Two servants do well and are rewarded with further opportunities of service in proportion to their success. Notice their modesty (“your mina has made”) and the much greater responsibility allotted to them.

Fear keeps the third man from doing anything, though he knows his master expects much. Nothing is said about the other seven. The parable is concerned with two classes: those who dare to invest what the master has entrusted to them and those who do not., 21

The punishment for not using what one has is to lose it, a principle of wide application. Those who use their spiritual opportunities find more, while those who do nothing about them lose what opportunity they do have.

verse_quote: put my money in the bank.
note: Lit. “on the table”—that is, of the money-exchange service at the temple, where a relatively risk-free and short-term investment yields a modest return as interest.
Luke reminds readers that Jesus’ destination is Jerusalem, where He will suffer rejection and death, leading to His resurrection (13:22, 33, 34; 17:11; 18:31; 19:11). See note on 9:51.
A village about two miles (3.2 km) from Jerusalem. Bethphage must be nearby; it is regarded as the outer limit of Jerusalem.
This can refer to a horse or a donkey; the other gospels make clear that it is a donkey. It has never been used and is therefore fit for a sacred purpose (Num. 19:2; 1 Sam. 6:7).

verse_quote: throwing their cloaks on the colt.
note: The clothing evidently serves as a saddle. The clothes on the road form a triumphal carpet., 36

This entry into Jerusalem fulfills prophecy (Zech. 9:9) and is a public claim to messiahship, but of a distinctive kind: the donkey is the animal of a man of peace and is associated with humility in Zechariah’s prophecy. A conquering king would ride a horse.

A quotation from Ps. 118:26 but with an explicit reference to the king. Luke alone has the words “peace” and “glory.” Thus the themes of this crowd’s welcoming praises echo the song sung by heaven’s hosts to shepherds at Jesus’ birth (2:14). Luke does not have “Hosanna” (representing the Hb. petition “Save!” but used as an expression of praise), which his Gentile readers might not understand.

The Pharisees do not want anything to disturb the peace and bring trouble from the Romans (John 11:45–52). Jesus’ widespread popularity in the days leading up to the Passover, the feast commemorating Israel’s liberation from Gentile (Egyptian) oppression, threatens to launch a revolutionary movement that will provoke brutal suppression by Rome.

Only Luke records Jesus’ lament as He draws near the city (cf. 13:34, 35). Jesus knows that the excitement of the crowds does not correspond to genuine spiritual perception of His messianic mission. Although the crowds speak of “peace” (v. 38), they fail to grasp the reconciliation with God that was their deepest need and Jesus’ central task. In a few days, the crowds will repudiate Him, and the ultimate result will be war, not peace, as God will use the Romans in A.D. 70 to judge the city that defied His Son., 42
A description of a typical siege of a city (Is. 29:1–4; 37:33). The embankment is erected as a protection for the invaders and a base from which to launch attacks.
