The city will be completely destroyed and the temple razed by Roman forces under Titus in A.D. 70. The people must live with the consequences of their rejection of God’s Messiah.

**your visitation.** God’s personal intervention to rescue His people in the person of the Messiah, Jesus (Gen. 50:24, 25; Ex. 4:31).

All four Gospels speak of Jesus’ driving traders out of the temple precincts, but the Synoptics (Matt. 21:12–16; Mark 11:15–18) place it at the end of Jesus’ ministry while John (John 2:12–22) places it at the beginning. The Gospel writers, therefore, are probably describing two cleansings (Mark 11:15 note).

The merchants in the temple courts are money-changers and sellers of sacrificial animals, although Luke mentions only the latter. Both serve worshipers who have traveled from a distance, providing blemish-free animals for offering and coins from Tyre, the only currency acceptable for the payment of tithes. It is convenient to have them close to the temple, but their presence in the temple courts themselves makes true worship difficult. The traders are in the court of the Gentiles, the only place Gentiles can go in the first century to pray to the only true God.

**19:45 entered the temple.** Malachi prophesied, “The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple,” purifying Israel’s worship like a refiner’s fire (Mal. 3:1–4).

**19:46 a house of prayer.** This is written in Is. 56:7, which promises Gentile foreigners that the temple “shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

The temple is a normal place for teaching. Jesus’ opposition now includes a new group—“the principal men of the people.” Evidently, prominent laypeople have now joined the priests and the scribes., 48

Jesus is bringing God’s good news at the very time His enemies are plotting against Him.

**chief priests ... scribes ... elders.** This may be a delegation from the Sanhedrin.

By driving the merchants out of the temple, Jesus directly insults the authority of the Sadducean chief priests who supervise the temple’s operations. Thus His actions imply a claim of authority superior to theirs, and the Sanhedrin’s representatives demand that He identify the source of His authority.
Jesus is not avoiding their question. John has testified that Jesus is the Messiah. If they answer Jesus’ question, they will have the answer to their own., 4
They are not concerned with the truth but with the consequences of their possible answers and the reaction of public opinion (19:48)., 6

Jesus will not overtly identify the source of His authority to men who evade an important religious question, the answer to which they already know. Yet the parable that He immediately tells contains His answer: “I will send my beloved son” (v. 13)., 8
The tenants are a vivid picture of Israel and its leaders, who have rejected persistently the prophets whom God sent to call them to repentance (2 Chr. 36:15, 16; Is. 3:13–15).

Normally, a landowner confronted with persistent refusal to pay and with abuse of his messengers would take strong measures. But just as this landowner keeps giving the tenants the opportunity for repentance, so God repeatedly reaches out to His rebellious people. As did Jesus’ earlier parable of the fig tree (13:6–9), this parable speaks of the last opportunity for Israel to bear for its owner the fruit that is His before judgment ensues.

Within the plot of the parable, apparently the tenants infer that the son’s arrival means that the owner has died. They apparently reasoned that with the heir out of the way, they can establish their own title to the land. Jesus is making the point that the nation has behaved outrageously toward God, and the leaders’ current plot to destroy Him (19:47) will lead only to their own destruction.

Jesus quotes Ps. 118:22, which uses architectural imagery to speak of the Lord’s exalting one whom Israel’s leaders (“builders”) have scorned and rejected. The psalm identifies the “cornerstone” as the keystone to the temple, so that the application to Jesus identifies Him with the new form of the end-time temple. The psalm goes on to identify this marvelously exalted “stone” as the blessed one “who comes in the name of the Lord” (118:26), in the words echoed by the crowds at Jesus’ triumphal entry a few days earlier (Luke 19:38). Peter later applies these words from the psalm to the Sanhedrin’s repudiation of Jesus (Acts 4:11; cf. 1 Pet. 2:4, 7).

**cornerstone.** Lit. “the head of the corner.” It is likely a large stone in the foundation of the temple, laid at the corner and determining the position of two walls. Or it may be the stone at the top of the corner binding the building together.

See note on Matt. 21:44 regarding temple language from Dan. 2.

**20:19** The religious teachers are hostile to Jesus but can find no way to do away with Him without arousing the rage of the people, who are “hanging on his words” (19:47, 48).
Clearly the “spies” hope to lure Jesus into saying something that will suggest insurrection against Rome, forcing the governor to arrest and punish Him.
The flattering approach is doubtless meant to put Jesus off guard, though the words themselves accurately describe Jesus’ complete integrity (see John 3:2).

The question is whether paying taxes to Rome is in accordance with God’s law (it is required by Roman law). From the questioners’ point of view, the answer has to put Jesus at odds with either the Romans, who would view the refusal to pay taxes as a criminal act, or the Jews, who resent the taxes because they represent the subjugation of God’s covenant people to a pagan Gentile empire.

Jesus asks for the silver coin that is the proper coinage for paying the tax, roughly equivalent to a day’s wage (15:8 note). It bears an image of the emperor with his titles of honor, including “Lord” and “Savior.”

**Whose likeness and inscription.** There is only one answer to Jesus’ question, and it opens the way for His unexpected reply. Jesus cannot be accused of disloyalty to either the Jews or the Romans. He makes it clear that there are duties owed to God but also duties to the state.

verse_quote: to God the things that are God’s.
note: Since Caesar’s image identifies the denarius as his property, Jesus may be alluding to Gen. 1:26, 27 to imply that human beings (including his deceitful interrogators) who bear God’s image must recognize that they are God’s property and thus render themselves to God in repentance and faith.

Luke mentions the Sadducees only here in his gospel but speaks of their beliefs and influence over the temple operations in Acts (4:1; 5:17; 23:6–9). None of their writings survive, so we know them only as their opponents saw them. They were conservative and aristocratic, and they counted the high priests among their ranks. They rejected the oral tradition of the Pharisees and found no basis for a doctrine of resurrection in the books of Moses, the portion of the OT that they valued most highly.

When a Jew died childless, his brother was required to marry the widow, and the first son would become the heir of the deceased (Deut. 25:5–10). The Sadducees clearly think that their story of a woman married in succession to seven brothers, in keeping with the law, makes nonsense of the doctrine of resurrection.

The Sadducees assume that if there is an afterlife, particularly a return to embodied existence through resurrection, it will simply replicate the conditions of this life. Jesus denies this. Marriage is an essential part of life in this age but not of life in the age to come. Therefore, the conundrum they pose is invalid.

At the resurrection, there will be a change in our physical nature, and believers will have resurrection bodies like that of Christ (1 Cor. 15:35–58 and notes). Jesus’ point is not that human beings will be exactly like angels, but that the mode of existence of angels, and in particular their immortality, provides a clue to the post-resurrection existence of believers, who will also be immortal (1 Cor. 15:42, 52–55). Marriage and procreation will no longer be necessary or appropriate. See theological note “The Last Resurrection” on p. 2040.

Before the addition of chapter and verse divisions, passages in Scripture were referred to by their content. Jesus draws an interesting proof from a well-known text in the second book of Moses (Ex. 3) that people continue to live after they have died (Mark 12:26 note).

verse_quote: not the God of the dead, but of the living.
note: Jesus implies that when God appeared to Moses, centuries after the death of the patriarchs, He still sustained a faithful and vital relationship with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God’s covenant commitment to His people means that physical death cannot ultimately overcome and eliminate them. Rather, death will be reversed in the end by the God who gives life.

Earlier generations were regarded in the first century as wiser than the present generation, and this opens the way for Jesus to pose a question of His own. Generally, sons are to be subordinate to their fathers (Ex. 20:12; Prov. 1:8), and in popular estimation David is greater than any of his descendants. How, then, can David call the Messiah his “Lord” (Ps. 110:1)? Jesus shows that the psalm implies that the Messiah is not simply the son of David; He is the Son of God and so David’s Lord. Jesus’ messiahship may be understood in part from His title “Son of David,” but His identity encompasses more than His descent from the royal lineage of David.

On the scribes’ love of popular acclaim, see Matt. 6:1–18. On their readiness to exploit the piety of needy widows, see note on Mark 12:40. Jesus’ critique of such religious hypocrites highlights the contrast between them and the widow whom He is about to recognize for her costly generosity (21:1–4).
In the court of the women, there were thirteen trumpet-shaped collection boxes with inscriptions showing the use to which donations would be put.

An unusual word (used only here in the NT) meaning “very poor.” Her total livelihood (v. 4) is two copper coins of the lowest value (text note). What makes her gift more valuable than those of the rich is not its amount but the strength of faith and devotion it expresses.
This is fulfilled during the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70.
False teachers will claim to be the Christ.

verse_quote: these things must first take place.
note:
Although the “wars and tumults” accompanying the siege and destruction of Jerusalem by Roman forces under the general Titus will be traumatic, those events do not signal that the consummation of history is imminent. International conflict and natural disasters will continue (vv. 10, 11), along with persecution of Jesus’ followers.

**the end.** The end of all things. Some sections of this discourse refer to the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 and others to Jesus’ coming at the end of the age (Mark 13:4 note).
Synagogues are centers for discipline as well as places of worship.
Persecution for the church also means opportunity to bear witness, as the book of Acts illustrates (Acts 4:8–12; 5:29–32; 13:44–48; 22:1–21).

This passage is a strong affirmation of God’s overriding control and sovereign care of His people. For some of His followers, there will be a martyr’s death; for others, deliverance. Either way, God is bringing His purposes to pass.

verse_quote: not a hair of your head will perish.
note: Although some will be put to death (v. 16), not even death itself can separate believers from God’s love in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:35–39).
This section refers to the destruction of the city, not the end time (v. 9 note).
People would normally flee to a walled city for shelter from an invading army, but Jerusalem is doomed. People must run away from it, not try to enter it.
Not meaningless suffering, but the divine penalty.
The siege of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 will bring extreme suffering. The devastation awaiting the city’s residents for repudiating God’s Messiah evokes Jesus’ earlier laments (13:34, 35; 19:41–44).

This may mean the time when the Gentiles will have their triumph over Israel, or the time when the gospel is preached to the Gentiles (Rom. 11:11, 12, 25–32), or both.

**fulfilled.** A divine purpose will be worked out (cf. Rom. 11:1–32).

In biblical prophecy, scenes of cosmic dissolution sometimes symbolize major shifts in covenantal epochs (Acts 2:19, 20), but here it seems that Jesus shifts the subject to the second coming of Christ (v. 9 note), which will precipitate the destruction of the present heaven and earth and the introduction of a new heaven and earth (Rev. 20:11; 21:1). The Son of Man’s glorious return will be preceded by signs that will puzzle many., 26

verse_quote: the Son of Man coming in a cloud.
note: Forty days after His resurrection, Jesus ascends in a cloud to heaven, fulfilling the vision in which Daniel saw “one like a son of man” coming with the clouds of heaven to receive His universal dominion from the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7:13, 14; Acts 1:9–11). At the end of the age, Jesus’ return as the Son of Man will be a coming in splendor to judge and to consummate His reign. Alternatively, this verse may refer to His coming in A.D. 70 to judge Jerusalem. See note on Matt. 24:29–31.

This word means “deliverance on payment of a price.” Jesus pays the price at Calvary, and He here looks forward to the final fulfillment of what that deliverance means, which includes the bodily resurrection of believers (Rom. 8:23; Phil. 3:20, 21).

After these sentences in Mark 13:28–31, Jesus draws a contrast between the signs that forecast Jerusalem’s impending destruction and the unpredictable timing of His second coming at the end of the age (Mark 13:32). This contrast, along with His statement that “this generation will not pass away until all this has taken place” (Luke 21:32), may suggest that Jesus is switching the topic back to the traumas of A.D. 70.

The appearance of leaves on the trees announces that summer is at hand. So the signs tell us that the kingdom is near, apparently in the transition from the old covenant to the new, signified by Jerusalem’s fall and the spread of the gospel among the Gentiles.

The Gk. word usually means all the people alive at a given time, but it can also mean all of a certain kind of people (e.g., wicked or righteous) or a particular racial or ethnic group. In Luke, “this generation” typically refers to those who resist God’s will (7:31; 11:29–32, 50, 51; 17:25), so Jesus seems to be predicting that human opposition to God’s kingdom will continue right to the consummation.

Since “that day” will come upon all the earth’s residents, Jesus has returned to the theme of His second coming and the end of time, which will spring “suddenly like a trap” not only on the ungodly but also on “you,” His disciples., 35

Watchfulness and prayer are Christian duties to the end of time (cf. 12:35–48).

**to escape all these things.** Although believers are not promised immunity from the woes of life in this fallen world and are assured that they will be persecuted for their faith (John 16:33; 2 Tim. 3:12), Jesus’ blood and righteousness will shield them from God’s wrath, which will come on the wicked at the end of history (3:7; 1 Thess. 1:10).

**to stand before the Son of Man.** This signifies salvation at the last day.

Jesus’ last days are spent teaching in Jerusalem, while at night He stays on the Mount of Olives nearby. The people’s eagerness to hear Him continues to thwart the desire of their leaders to destroy Him (22:2; cf. 19:47, 48; 20:6, 19, 26)., 38

Strictly speaking, Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are different but immediately successive festivals (Num. 28:16–25), although leaven is to be removed from Israel’s dwellings before the evening on which the Passover is observed (Ex. 12:14–20). In NT times, the names are used interchangeably. The feast commemorates the great deliverance of Israel from Egypt (Ex. 12:17; Mark 14:1 note).

The chief priests have the political power among the Jews, and they, not the Pharisees, lead the final opposition to Jesus.

**feared the people.** See note on 21:38.
Satan takes control of Judas (John 13:2), and it is Judas who seeks the chief priests, not they who seek him. The “officers” of the temple guard are mostly Levites.

The Gk. term means “hand over.” It is also used to speak of the Father’s “giving up” His own Son as our sacrifice (Rom. 8:32) and of Christ “giving up” Himself for us (Eph. 5:2). But in the Gospels, where it refers to Judas’s treachery, “betray” is the fitting translation.

**22:6 in the absence of a crowd.** Access to Jesus’ whereabouts through Judas, an “insider,” will enable the temple leadership to take Jesus into custody without immediately provoking the outrage of the people who eagerly listen to His teaching. See note on 21:38.
According to Ex. 12:5, the animal can be a lamb or a young goat. It is killed at twilight (Ex. 12:6).
Jesus is ready to die but at the time of His own choosing. This may be the reason for the way Jesus makes arrangements for the feast. None of the disciples know where they will eat it.

A man carrying a pitcher of water will stand out because in Jesus’ day pitchers are used by women; men carry water in skins. As with the colt on which Jesus entered Jerusalem a few days earlier (19:29–34), the way that He directs His disciples to the room for their Passover observance may be intended to teach Jesus’ omniscience.
The normal posture at such a meal. The diners lean on their left elbows, facing the table with their feet away from it, and eat with the right hand.

Aware that His suffering and death are imminent (12:50; 20:13–15; Mark 14:8; John 13:1), Jesus has an intense desire for fellowship with His disciples at the Passover.

**until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.** Jesus’ abstinence from the Passover and its wine “until the kingdom of God comes” (v. 18) looks far ahead to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:6–9). In preliminary forms, God’s kingdom is present in Jesus’ earthly ministry (17:20, 21) and will arrive in escalated form with His enthronement in heaven and bestowal of the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:3, 6–8; 2:32–36). The kingdom’s consummate expression awaits the return of the king, Jesus., 16
At the Passover meal, each person drinks four cups of red wine. The wine is diluted, usually three parts of water to one of wine.

verse_quote: until the kingdom of God comes.
note: This future anticipation is an important aspect of the Lord’s Supper as a sacrament; it points forward to the second coming of Christ (1 Cor. 11:26).

There has been much discussion of these words (Matt. 26:26 note). The verb “is” in this instance does not mean “is identical with” or “is transformed into” but rather “represents,” “signifies,” or perhaps “conveys.” See theological note “The Lord’s Supper” on p. 2032.

**in remembrance of me.** The one thing Jesus has commanded His followers to do as a remembrance of Him refers to His death, underlining the centrality of the cross for the Christian faith.

By His death, Jesus offers the sacrifice that ratifies the new covenant of Jer. 31:31, which exceeds and replaces the cov­enant ratified in sacrificial blood at Sinai (Ex. 24:3–8; cf. Matt. 26:28; Mark 14:24).

Jesus immediately speaks of betrayal by one of those at the table. That Judas is enjoying table fellowship with Jesus makes his crime all the worse. Jesus will fulfill prophecy and go as it has been decreed (v. 37; 24:26, 27; Acts 1:16–20), but this does not lessen the guilt of the one who betrays Him. See Gen. 50:20.

Although Mark (10:35–45) and Matthew (20:20–28) record an earlier argument over greatness engendered by James’s and John’s request for preeminent places in Christ’s kingdom, only Luke reports the shameful revival of this dispute as Jesus’ thoughts are dominated by His suffering and sacrificial death in the hours to come. Their rivalry shows how far even the Twelve are from understanding the servant’s mission that Jesus came to fulfill.
A number of kings in antiquity took the title “benefactor,” often with little justification.

The disciples must serve, as Jesus does. At this meal He displays His readiness to perform the lowliest of service by washing their feet, the humiliating task of a slave that none of the disciples condescends to do (John 13:3–16)., 27

That the disciples should serve rather than seek greatness does not mean they will go unnoticed. Jesus makes clear that He knows how they have stood with Him and that there will be a place for them in the kingdom. They are promised a wonderful future that includes judging the tribes of Israel (v. 30). In fact, because all believers are united by God’s grace to Christ the king, they will rule with Him (Rev. 5:9, 10) and judge angels (1 Cor. 6:3).

The repetition conveys solemnity and emphasis, tinged with sadness and rebuke (10:41; 13:34).

**demanded to have you.** The word “you” is plural. Satan has asked permission to trouble all the disciples. Notice that Satan has no power to act outside the area God allows him (cf. Job 1:6–12; 2:1–7).

Here the word “you” is singular.

**when you have turned again.** Despite Peter’s protestation of loyalty and courage, he will deny Jesus three times that very night. Yet Jesus’ prayer is effective: despite his cowardice, Peter’s faith will not utterly fail, and his turning again is a certainty, not a mere possibility.

**strengthen your brothers.** When Peter has come through the trial, he is to strengthen others. The complete forgiveness and restoration that Jesus will grant after Peter’s denials will be shown in the renewed assignment to feed and tend his Savior’s sheep (John 21:15–17).

In their earlier missions, the Twelve and the seventy-two traveled light and received God’s extraordinary provision through the hospitality of those who received them (9:3; 10:4). In the new era of gospel advance precipitated by Jesus’ death, resurrection, and ascension, however, heralds of the kingdom should not expect extraordinary providential provision. They should expect ordinary providence and plan accordingly for their daily needs.

**22:36 sword.** This is probably not meant literally (cf. vv. 49–51; Matt. 26:51, 52) but is a way of saying that they face a dangerous future.
Jesus Himself faces the necessary fulfillment of Is. 53:12, and His followers will surely experience resistance and persecution.
The disciples take the words about the sword literally, but Jesus’ reply means, “Enough of that sort of talk” (cf. v. 51).

Gethsemane (Mark 14:32), meaning “olive press,” is the name of a grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron brook from Jerusalem’s eastern wall (John 18:1).

**Pray.** Unlike those of Mark and Matthew, Luke’s account does not mention Peter, James, and John (who sleep while Jesus prays). Luke’s emphasis is on Jesus’ prayer, not the disciples’ failings.
In Jesus’ day people generally pray standing (18:11, 13), but at this solemn time Jesus kneels (cf. Eph. 3:14).

A symbol of suffering and divine anger (Is. 51:17; Ezek. 23:33). Earlier that evening, Jesus identified the cup of the new covenant, which He offered to His disciples, with His blood (v. 20).

**not my will.** As one who has taken upon Himself a complete human nature, it is natural for Jesus to shrink from the horror of the cross, a horror magnified by His knowledge that in dying He will be forsaken by God and experience the weight of divine anger on sin, though He is Himself utterly innocent and righteous. Nevertheless, Jesus is determined to follow the will of His Father for the redemption of His people (John 6:38, 39; Heb. 10:5–10).

Luke alone tells of the angel who strengthens Jesus and of the sweat “like great drops of blood.” These verses are absent in many early manuscripts (text note), so they may not have been written by Luke. As with all places in Scripture where the text is in question, the inclusion or omission of these verses does not affect any Christian doctrine. See topical article “New Testament Textual Criticism” on p. 2369., 44
The kiss is a common greeting (1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14), and to use it in this way is a horrible form of betrayal (2 Sam. 20:9, 10).

Still misunderstanding Jesus’ earlier word about obtaining a sword in preparation for future hostility (vv. 36–38), the apostles momentarily stand ready to defend Jesus with violence. One wounds the high priest’s servant before Jesus issues a sharp rebuke to His would-be defenders, as He did to James and John outside a Samaritan town (9:52–55). All four Gospels record this incident, and John gives the name of the swordsman (Simon Peter) and his victim (Malchus; John 18:10). Luke alone records that Jesus heals His enemy’s severed ear.
A furtive arrest at night suits this effort of the forces of spiritual darkness (cf. Eph. 6:12; Col. 1:13).

Jesus is taken first to the high priest who ordered His arrest. All four Gospels give more space to the trial than to the crucifixion. They are answering questions about why the Jews condemned Jesus and why the Romans executed Him and are also bringing out His identity as the Son of God and king of the Jews.

**Peter was following at a distance.** John 18:15, 16 indicates that “another disciple” (perhaps John) obtains access for Peter into the high priest’s courtyard, but in all four Gospels the spotlight is on Peter, who confidently claimed before His denial that his loyalty toward Jesus overshadowed everyone else’s. The distance that Peter keeps anticipates the denials by which he will disavow association with Jesus.

All four Gospels say that the first challenge comes from a servant girl, but the second variously from the same girl (Mark 14:69), a different girl (Matt. 26:71), or a man (Luke 22:58). Servants were around a fire in a courtyard; a challenge from any of them would be taken up by the others, and there would have been several voices challenging Peter. The threefold denial fulfills the prediction of v. 34.
Jesus is evidently left to a guard of soldiers who physically and psychologically torment Him.

Jesus was earlier acclaimed as a prophet of God (7:16, 39) and performed miracles reminiscent of those associated with Elijah and Elisha (7:11–17; 9:12–17). Now His captors mockingly demand that He prove His prophetic gift by identifying those who struck Him, without seeing them. Their mocking echoes Satan’s taunt, “If you are the Son of God” (4:3).

No single gospel gives a complete account of Jesus’ trial. It is clear that there were two main stages: the Jews tried Him before the Sanhedrin and obtained a verdict that He was a blasphemer and deserved to die. However, only the Romans had the right to execute Him, and they would not execute a man for blasphemy against the God of Israel. There had to be a further trial before the Romans to try to establish some violation of Roman law that would deserve capital punishment.

**22:66 day.** Jewish trials had to be held in the daytime. Mark indicates, however, that an unofficial hearing in the chief priest’s home took place during the night (Mark 14:53–65, 72) and preceded the public meeting of the Sanhedrin (Mark 15:1), which Luke reports here.

Luke does not speak of a formal accusation or of a trial according to proper procedure. The Sanhedrin simply requires Jesus to incriminate Himself according to their understanding of the Messiah. This He declines to do, as they will not believe Him.

**22:68 you will not answer.** The opposition of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, with a few exceptions (23:50, 51; John 3:1; 7:50–52; 19:38, 39), is so entrenched that they simply refuse to respond to questions from Jesus that challenge them (20:3–8, 39, 40, 44).

Jesus does say that a change is coming “from now on,” when as the Son of Man He will be in the place of highest honor in heaven, fulfilling Dan. 7:14 and Ps. 110:1. His pouring out of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost constitutes a public display on earth of His enthronement at God’s right hand in heaven (Acts 2:33).

Jesus’ conflation of OT texts brings together the glorious “one like a son of man” who will rule all peoples with the priest king whom David calls his “Lord” (20:41–44). The Sanhedrin rightly infers that He is claiming to be Son of God in a uniquely exalted sense (1:31–35; 3:22; 9:35).

Jesus has conceded to the Sanhedrin’s charge that He claimed to be the Son of God, and as far as they are concerned He is guilty of blasphemy (cf. Matt. 26:65; John 10:30–33). Persuading the Romans to act will require a different charge, but for the Sanhedrin the matter is over. Jesus is guilty in their eyes, and it remains only to secure His execution.
Not all of the members of the Sanhedrin are needed, but their united front will impress Pilate with their seriousness.

A curiously imprecise charge. Certainly, Jesus has taken issue with rabbinic tradition, but that will be of no concern to the Roman authorities. Aware of Jesus’ popularity with ordinary Jews (19:48; 21:38), the Sanhedrin’s spokesmen will go on to charge that His teaching “stirs up the people,” hinting that He is inciting armed insurrection against the empire—a danger that the governor cannot ignore.

**forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar.** Jesus did the opposite, commanding that what is Caesar’s be rendered to Caesar (20:25).

**saying that he ... is Christ, a king.** Jesus specifically refuses to use the title, although He does acknowledge that He is the Son of God (22:67–69). The Sanhedrin deliberately places a political-military connotation on these titles to give Pilate the impression that Jesus threatens Rome’s occupation of Judea. In the senses that the Sanhedrin intends to convey, all the charges are false.

In one sense, Jesus is king of the Jews, but not in the sense in which Pilate understands the title. His answer is therefore ambiguous (cf. John 18:33–38). Without denying the title, Jesus distances Himself from its political and militant associations. From this reply, Pilate concludes that Jesus is no revolutionary (v. 4).

In the Roman Empire, a trial was usually held in the province where the offense was committed, but it could be transferred to the province from which the accused came. Pilate seizes on this to send Jesus to Herod Antipas, apparently trying to evade pressure from the Sanhedrin to execute Jesus, who is clearly not guilty of a capital offense under Roman law (vv. 4, 14–16). Only Luke mentions this temporary change of venue to Herod’s legal authority as tetrarch of Galilee.

Herod Antipas earlier ordered the execution of John the Baptist (3:19, 20; 9:7–9; cf. 13:31). His interest in Jesus’ case has nothing to do with justice but is driven by curiosity to see a miracle like those that have been reported to him. Therefore, Herod is the only person to whom Jesus refuses to speak.
Herod mocks Jesus by dressing Him royally, ridiculing the charge that He is Israel’s anointed king.
These political leaders’ complicity in the conspiracy “against the Lord and his Anointed” fulfills Ps. 2:1, 2, as the early Christians recognized (Acts 4:25–28).

Under Roman law, a person could be beaten and warned to be more careful in the future. Pilate is evidently hoping that this will placate the Jews and enable him to release one he knows to be innocent.

**23:17** The custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover is not attested outside the Gospels, but this sort of thing was widely done at this time, and there is nothing improbable about it. This sentence may not occur in Luke’s original (text note), but the custom and expectation that it describes appear in Mark 15:6, and it may be that an earlier copyist, who knew Mark’s gospel well, inadvertently entered it into Luke’s recounting of the Passion.
The crowds clamor for Barabbas, a man otherwise unknown. His name means “son of the father” in Aramaic.

Ironically, Barabbas is guilty of the defiant, disruptive crimes against the empire of which the Sanhedrin falsely accuse Jesus. Luke repeats Barabbas’s crimes in v. 25, in connection with Pilate’s release of that terrorist “for whom they asked.”

Crucifixion is Rome’s cruelest form of execution, reserved for slaves and the most violent of criminals. It involves a slow death by asphyxiation as the victim is suspended by his arms and supported by his feet until fatigue prevents his drawing breath into his lungs. The public exposure adds shame to the physical torment.
The hostile forcefulness of the Jewish leaders and the feeble acquiescence of the Roman governor, who knows that Jesus is innocent (v. 14), are repeatedly emphasized.

It is customary for the condemned to carry the horizontal crossbeam to the site of the crucifixion. Jesus starts to carry His cross (John 19:17), but He is weakened by the heavy scourging that Roman soldiers have already inflicted (Mark 15:15), which lacerated flesh and drew blood. The soldiers conscript a passerby named Simon, from Cyrene in North Africa. His sons apparently were known in the early church (Mark 15:21 note).

Only Luke records this lament of the people, especially women, over Jesus’ suffering. Other gospels report that the fickle crowds who had welcomed Jesus’ entrance into Jerusalem a few days earlier joined their leaders’ demands for His execution (Mark 15:8–15; Matt. 27:20–23). But Luke notes that among the many common folk who have listened eagerly to Jesus’ teaching that week (19: 48; 20:6, 19, 26; 21:38; 22:2), there are still many who are shocked and saddened by the unjust verdict against Him.

These are local people, not pilgrims from Galilee. Jesus is concerned for them, not for Himself, and turns their attention to the terrible troubles that will come upon the land and its capital city (21:20–24).

Since childlessness was an occasion of shame typically associated with God’s displeasure (1:7, 24, 25), only the direst disaster could make barrenness a blessing. Worse than inability to bear children is seeing one’s children slaughtered, as will occur when Jerusalem falls in A.D. 70 (21:23, 24).
Israel’s prophets predicted that when God’s righteous wrath is unleashed, people will seek shelter from it, even at the cost of being crushed by mountains (Hos. 10:8; Is. 2:19; cf. Rev. 6:16, 17).
Evidently a proverbial saying, possibly meaning that if Jesus (who is innocent) is crucified, what will happen to the Jewish leaders and populace (who unjustly demanded His death)?

From the Aramaic _golgotha_,(Gk. _kranion_,Latin _calvaria_), meaning “a skull.” All four Gospels say that Jesus is crucified between two criminals; in His death, He “is numbered with the transgressors,” as He foretold (22:37; Is. 53:12).

Both Jews and Romans. The mercy expressed in Jesus’ request to His Father will reappear in the dying prayer of Stephen, the first recorded martyr after Pentecost (Acts 7:60).

**they know not what they do.** The ignorance of the Jewish and Gentile conspirators against the Lord and His Messiah (Acts 4:25–28) does not excuse them, but it leaves the door to repentance open (1 Tim. 1:13–15; cf. 1 Cor. 2:8). This verse is absent in many early manuscripts (text note). See note on 22:43, 44.

**his garments.** The clothing of a crucified person was normally given to those who carried out the execution. In this way, Ps. 22:18 (cited in John 19:24) is fulfilled.

The rulers, not the people, are sneering. They speak of “the Christ” and the “Chosen One.” Although Jesus seems not to have used either title often, He implicitly granted the correctness of Peter’s confession that He is the Christ of God (9:20–22) and did not disavow the title when interrogated by the Sanhedrin (22:67–70). The Father’s voice at the transfiguration identified Jesus as the Father’s “Chosen One” (9:35).

**save himself.** The suffering Messiah’s tormenters in Ps. 22:7, 8 taunt Him that God will rescue Him—if He actually enjoys God’s favor.

Formally, “King of the Jews” states the crime for which execution was imposed. In God’s providence, it also correctly identifies Jesus and implies the character of His kingship as He enters His dominion through suffering.
At first, both criminals crucified with Jesus echo the insulting taunts of the Jewish leaders and Roman soldiers (Mark 15:32), but Jesus’ response persuades one that He is innocent.
This request indicates some measure of trust. The man believes that Jesus is not about to be annihilated in death but is going to a heavenly kingdom.

If the repentant criminal envisions bodily resurrection in a distant future kingdom, he is not wrong; but Jesus promises more immediate communion with Himself even in the interim between physical death and Christ’s return and the final resurrection. See theological note “The Intermediate State” on p. 2109.

**Paradise.** A Persian word for “garden,” which came to mean “the place of the righteous dead” (2 Cor. 12:3; Rev. 2:7).

verse_quote: about the sixth hour ... until the ninth hour.
note:
From about noon until three P.M., reckoning the hours of the day from dawn.

**darkness.** This is a supernatural darkness, perhaps a fulfillment of Joel 2:30, 31, to be cited by Peter on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:19, 20).

Although the temple has several curtains, this is probably the curtain separating the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place, the outer chamber of the sanctuary structure. Mark 15:38 notes that the curtain is torn “from top to bottom,” indicating a divine act (the curtain was approximately thirty feet [9 m] high). Jesus’ death opens the way into the presence of God (Heb. 10:19–22), thereby making the temple obsolete as the place of atonement for sins. At this point, well before the temple’s destruction in A.D. 70 (Luke 21:20–24), God inaugurates a new temple composed of living “stones” (i.e., believers) built on Jesus, the foundation (1 Pet. 2:4, 5; Eph. 2:20–22; Acts 2:3 note).

Matthew and Mark emphasize how terrible Jesus’ death is. Luke does not deny this but records Jesus’ words, quoting Ps. 31:6, thereby showing that His death is in accordance with the will of the Father.

**breathed his last.** This is not the usual way of referring to death. None of the Gospels employs standard terminology for Jesus’ death.

The way He died showed Him to be “innocent” (Gk. “righteous”). Matthew and Mark have “Son of God”; in this context, the two terms may have had similar meaning in the centurion’s mind, although Matthew and Mark would expect their readers to grasp a fuller sense than the centurion himself perceived (Mark 15:39 note).
A sign of grief. The crowd came to be entertained, but Jesus’ death disturbs them.

Luke does not say what effect the death has on the disciples who “stood at a distance” to witness it. Their aloofness may allude to the bleakest lament psalm (Ps. 88:18) and contrasts with the readiness of Joseph of Arimathea to risk his reputation and more by arranging Jesus’ burial (23:50–53).

Joseph of Arimathea is mentioned in all four Gospels as taking the leading role in Jesus’ burial. The location of Arimathea is uncertain (Mark 15:43 note). Joseph is a member of the Sanhedrin and must have been absent when the vote to execute Jesus was taken, for “all” agreed to it (Mark 14:64). That he is “looking for the kingdom of God” (v. 51) means that he is a disciple of Jesus, as Matthew states (Matt. 27:57)., 51

The linen cloth is a shroud (placed over the linen strips mentioned in John 19:40).

**a tomb cut in stone.** A rock tomb generally holds several bodies (Mark 15:46 note), but this one is empty.
Friday, the day on which people prepare for the Sabbath, which begins at sundown (John 19:14 note).

There is not time on Friday to do all that Jesus’ followers would have liked for His burial. The women take note of where the body is laid, evidently to know where to come when the Sabbath is over to complete the burial process. Joseph and Nicodemus place a considerable quantity of myrrh and aloes with the body as they lay it in the tomb (John 19:38, 39), but the women want to make their own contribution.

**On the Sabbath they rested.** Even in their heart-wrenching sorrow, the women observe God’s command to rest on the seventh day (Ex. 20:10, 11)., 56

Each gospel deals with the resurrection in its own way, though none describes how it happened. Some things are clear in all four: the empty tomb, the slowness of the disciples to believe that the resurrection had happened, and the prominence of women in the first appearances. But each gospel also has something that does not appear in the others. Luke includes the account of the walk to Emmaus and related events.

**24:1 the first day of the week.** This begins at sunset on Saturday, so the women have had the hours of darkness to complete their preparations before setting out for the tomb at daybreak.

In the first century, a stone tomb was closed by rolling a stone in front of the opening (Mark 15:46 note). Matthew notes that a seal was placed on the stone, signifying that Roman imperial authority would punish anyone who disturbed it (Matt. 27:66)., 3
Spirit messengers (angels; v. 23) sent by God appear to be men, but their dazzling clothing shows that they are not human beings (Acts 1:10).

As the angels remind the women, Jesus told His followers repeatedly that He “must” suffer, die, and be raised on the third day (9:22, 44; 17:25; 18:32, 33; 22:37). This was God’s sovereign plan announced in the OT (24:25, 26, 44–47; Acts 17:2, 3)., 7

There is a large group of Jesus’ followers in Jerusalem, in addition to the eleven apostles. Many are Galileans who traveled to Jerusalem for the Passover, including those who accompanied His triumphal entry (19:37).

Mary Magdalene is the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:10–18). She is mentioned in all four Gospels in connection with the crucifixion and the resurrection; but otherwise we hear of her only in 8:2, where we learn that Jesus had exorcised seven demons from her.

In general, the testimony of women was not highly regarded by first-century Jews, and some rabbinic tradition deemed their testimony inadmissible in a court of law. This mindset lies behind the misgivings later expressed by two disciples en route to Emmaus (vv. 22–24).

verse_quote: saw the linen cloths by themselves.
note: This detail exposes the mistake of the rumor later circulated by the Sanhedrin, that Jesus’ body was stolen (Matt. 28:11–15). Peter’s marveling is ambiguous, indicating astonishment or confusion, but not necessarily faith.
The exact site is not known, although Luke gives its distance (“about seven miles” [11 km]) from Jerusalem.

This appears to mean that God has prevented them from recognizing Jesus at this time. When they have been persuaded from Moses and the prophets to expect the Messiah’s suffering and resurrection, they will be ready to recognize Him (see 16:29–31).
Cleopas is not mentioned elsewhere, nor is his companion identified.

verse_quote: a prophet mighty in deed and word.
note: Stephen will describe Moses in similar terms (Acts 7:22). Luke will summarize the contents of this gospel, his “first book,” as “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts 1:1).
The disciples place the principal responsibility for Jesus’ death on their own people, not on the Romans.
The word means to set free by paying a price. Clearly, the two are thinking of the political deliverance of their nation.
The women’s report of the empty tomb (confirmed by men) and the vision of angels amazes these men but does nothing to alleviate their sadness (v. 17) or dashed hopes (v. 21).

verse_quote: O foolish ones, and slow of heart.
note: Their failure to embrace the Scriptures’ predictions of the Messiah’s suffering and subsequent glory is attributable not to the Bible’s obscurity but to their spiritual blindness.
See vv. 44–47. Peter gives a similar outline of the message of the OT in 1 Pet. 1:10, 11.

The first two sections of the Hebrew OT canon are the books of Moses (Genesis–Deuteronomy) and the “Prophets,” which in the Jewish reckoning include historical books such as Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings as well as prophetical writings such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Minor Prophets. Throughout these portions of God’s Word, Jesus shows them promises and foreshadowings of Himself and His mission. See note on 24:44.

verse_quote: took the bread ... blessed ... broke ... gave it to them.
note: These were actions a host performs at a meal, but they are also reminiscent of Jesus’ institution of the Lord’s Supper a few evenings earlier (22:19; cf. 9:16).
This is by divine action (cf. v. 16).
Even before they recognize Jesus, His opening of the Scriptures to show them His suffering and subsequent glory replaces their despair with faith and joy.
They had not believed the women (v. 11), but an appearance to Simon Peter is more convincing.

The sudden appearance of Jesus among them, although the doors were locked (John 20:19), indicates that Jesus’ resurrection body is not subject to the same limitations that our present mortal and “lowly bodies” are (Phil. 3:21; 1 Cor. 15:42–57).

verse_quote: startled ... frightened ... thought they saw a spirit.
note: Despite the testimony of Simon and the two who returned from Emmaus, confusion and doubt persist (cf. Matt. 28:17). Consequently, Jesus provides “many proofs” (Acts 1:3) that He has risen bodily, overwhelming their unbelief and qualifying them to bear eyewitness testimony to His resurrection (Acts 1:21, 22; 2:32; Luke 1:2)., 38
That is, to see the nail marks. His risen body, though gloriously transformed, still bears the scars of His suffering (John 20:24–29).
The risen Christ eats and drinks, proving that He is not merely a visionary appearance (see Acts 1:3)., 43

The word “must” indicates that the Messiah’s suffering and resurrection, together with the blessings that flow from those events to all nations, are central to the purposes of God revealed in the OT. Therefore, God’s sovereign will mandates that those Scriptures be fulfilled.

**the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms.** The threefold division of the Hebrew Bible. As the first book in the third section of the Hebrew canon, “Psalms” stands for all the books in that section (called “the Writings”). Jesus is saying that every part of Scripture bears witness to Him.

Jesus shows them the way to understand the Bible, but He also removes the spiritual blindness and slowness of heart that has hindered their understanding and acceptance of its message. Christ’s death and resurrection were foretold in the OT (v. 26 note). In addition, the calling of people to repentance and remission of sin were foretold, as was the fact that this message of salvation would go out from Jerusalem to all nations (v. 47; cf. Acts 1:8). These blessings are all based on Christ’s atoning death and glorious resurrection.

The apostles (and preachers, who are their fallible successors) are not to produce some novel concepts of their own but to bear witness to what God has done. The apostles, uniquely, are Jesus’ witnesses (Acts 1:8) to testify to His resurrection (Acts 1:21, 22; 2:32; 3:15; 5:32; 10:39, 41; 13:31). Only their words are inspired, and the task of church leaders is to remain faithful to the apostolic testimony of the Scriptures and not to claim the same authority for themselves. With the death of the last apostle at the end of the first century, special revelation ceased, though the Holy Spirit continues to bless His people with the understanding of His Word.

The risen Jesus will send what His Father has promised, the gift of the Holy Spirit (Joel 2:28–32; Acts 2:1–4; cf. Is. 44:3, 8).

**stay in the city.** As Acts 1:5 shows, this command implies that the promised descent of the Spirit from the Father will occur “not many days from now.” It also means that they will need the Spirit’s power “from on high” (Is. 32:15) to fulfill their mission as witnesses.

Luke gives no time indication here, but elsewhere he states that the ascension takes place forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1:3).

**Bethany.** A village on the Mount of Olives about two miles (3 km) east of Jerusalem (John 11:18).

Luke’s account of the ascension is a brief but fitting conclusion to his gospel, which is an account of “all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up” (Acts 1:1, 2). Luke provides a more detailed ascension account at the beginning of his second book (Acts 1:9–11). The ascension marks the end of the work Jesus came to do on earth and the beginning of what He continues to do in and through the church. See theological note “The Ascension of Christ.”

Whatever their view of Jesus in earlier days, they now recognize His divinity and worship Him. The separation does not bring sadness but “great joy,” as the angel of the Lord promised at Jesus’ birth (2:10, 11).
The gospel ends as it began, in Jerusalem with the worship of God.
